RulePack.Name: Fortify Secure Coding Rules, Community, Cloud

StructuralRule.Predicate:
/* cases handled: global_sec_http_op_sec_http, global_sec_https_op_sec_http, global_nosec_http_op_sec_http,global_nosec_https_op_sec_http case global_sec_http_op_sec_http: Global security with basic auth defined Global server with HTTP enabled Operation security defined with basic auth (overrides global) Operation server with HTTP enabled (overrides global) case global_sec_https_op_sec_http: Global security with basic auth defined Global server with HTTPS enabled Operation security defined with basic auth (overrides global) Operation server with HTTP enabled (overrides global) case global_nosec_http_op_sec_http: Global security not defined Global server with HTTP enabled Operation security defined with basic auth (overrides global) Operation server with HTTP enabled (overrides global) case global_nosec_https_op_sec_http: Global security not defined Global server with HTTPS enabled Operation security defined with basic auth (overrides global) Operation server with HTTP enabled (overrides global)
common case in the above is that an operation has overridden both global security requirement configuration and server HTTP value
Rule logic: rule must identify operation with both basic auth and http server config */
ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "openapi" and value matches "3.*" ] and pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "paths" and value is [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name matches "/.*" and value is [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)get|post|patch|delete|options|head|trace|put" and value is [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "servers" and value is [ ConfigArray: items contains [ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "url" and value matches "http://.*" ]* ] ] ] and pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "security"]* ]* ] ] ] ] ]

StructuralRule.Predicate: /* SSE, Confidential, encryption at host usually all have a vm defined with the disk encryption set defined inside the os_disk block and not in a vm extension block. if we detect one vm block and one vm extension block we assume that they are related because we are unable to match and resolve references. This will cause some false negatives when more than one machine is defined in the same file. */ ConfigMap: (pairs contains [ConfigPair: value is [ConfigBlock: blocktype == "resource" and ( labels[0] == "azurerm_linux_virtual_machine" or labels[0] == "azurerm_windows_virtual_machine" ) and ( attributes contains [ ConfigBlock: blocktype == "os_disk" and ( not attributes contains [ ConfigPair : name == "disk_encryption_set_id" or name == "secure_vm_disk_encryption_set_id" ] or attributes contains [ ConfigPair : (name == "disk_encryption_set_id" or name == "secure_vm_disk_encryption_set_id") and ( value is empty or value is null ) ]* ) ]* ) ]] and not pairs contains [ConfigPair: value is [ConfigBlock: blocktype == "resource" and labels[0] == "azurerm_virtual_machine_extension" ] ]) or pairs contains [ConfigPair: value is [ConfigBlock: blocktype == "resource" and ( labels[0] == "azurerm_virtual_machine_extension" and attributes contains [ ConfigPair : name == "settings" and not value matches ".*KeyEncryptionKeyURL.*" ]* ) ] ]

StructuralRule.Notes:
Rule requires scripting to parse destination port ranges as an arbitrary number of ports/ranges can be declared. Regex is used but it is pretty nasty. The regex has had to be a little redundant to capture cases like the following:
destination_port_range: 1-50 <-- This should trigger because port 22 is in range destination_port_range: 1-20, 333-3390 <-- This should trigger because port 3389 is in the second range destination_port_range: 1-20, 333-444, 22 <-- This should trigger because port 22 is explicitly specified
The regex has had to be written in a way to ensure that the lower end of the range is not partially matched. For example 36-100 could be improperly matched as 6-100 if the regex engine drops off the first digit (3). To ensure this does not happen, the regex is made to look for a non-digit to start off the pattern matching for the lower bound of the range. ([^/d]...). This handles ranges in the middle of the input string but not at the start, this is why we have another seemingly similar regex but only with string start (^) character match.
StructuralRule.VulnSubcategory: Improper Security Group Network Access Control
StructuralRule.Predicate: ConfigMap : pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(azure\.azcollection\.)?azure_rm_securitygroup" and value is [ ConfigMap : pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name == "rules" and value is [ ConfigArray: items contains [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "source_address_prefix" and value is [ConfigConcrete: value is "*" or value matches ".*/0" ]* ] and pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "access" and value is [ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)allow" ]* ] and pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "direction" and value is [ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)inbound" ]* ] and (pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "destination_port_range" and value is [ConfigConcrete: value matches ".*(22|3389).*" or value matches"(.*[^\d]+\d{1,3}|3389|[0-2][0-9]{3}|33[0-7][0-9]|3[0-2][0-9]{2}|338[0-8])-(\d{5,}|3389|[3-9][3-9]9[0-9]|3[4-9][0-9]{2}|[4-9][0-9]{3}).*" or value matches"(^\d{1,3}|3389|[0-2][0-9]{3}|33[0-7][0-9]|3[0-2][0-9]{2}|338[0-8])-(\d{5,}|3389|[3-9][3-9]9[0-9]|3[4-9][0-9]{2}|[4-9][0-9]{3}).*" or value matches "^(21|20|22|[0-1][0-9]|\d)-([2-9]{2}|[3-9][0-9]|\d{3,}).*" or value matches ".*[^\d]+(21|20|22|[0-1][0-9]|\d)-([2-9]{2}|[3-9][0-9]|\d{3,}).*" ]* ] or pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name == "destination_port_range" and value is [ConfigArray: items contains [ConfigConcrete: value matches ".*(22|3389).*" or value matches"(.*[^\d]+\d{1,3}|3389|[0-2][0-9]{3}|33[0-7][0-9]|3[0-2][0-9]{2}|338[0-8])-(\d{5,}|3389|[3-9][3-9]9[0-9]|3[4-9][0-9]{2}|[4-9][0-9]{3}).*" or value matches"(^\d{1,3}|3389|[0-2][0-9]{3}|33[0-7][0-9]|3[0-2][0-9]{2}|338[0-8])-(\d{5,}|3389|[3-9][3-9]9[0-9]|3[4-9][0-9]{2}|[4-9][0-9]{3}).*" or value matches "^(21|20|22|[0-1][0-9]|\d)-([2-9]{2}|[3-9][0-9]|\d{3,}).*" or value matches ".*[^\d]+(21|20|22|[0-1][0-9]|\d)-([2-9]{2}|[3-9][0-9]|\d{3,}).*" ]* ] ] ) ] ] ] and not pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name == "state" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)absent" ] ] ] ]

StructuralRule.Notes:
- SQL Server can have auditing enabled (and this then forces auditing on any database contained by the server) - SQL Databases can have auditing enabled (this only affects that certain database)
This rule will highlight the absence of auditingsettings for sql server only and a different rule should be created for databases (types : databases|Microsoft.Sql/servers/databases). The reason being that there is no simple way to relate a database declaration directly to a sql database without parsing and storing the dependency reference for a database and checking whether the server has been declared with auditingsettings. Furthermore, it is possible to declare audittingsettings on the same layer in a resource array and use the name variable to indicate the containing database. Again this requires parsing and reference resolution.
StructuralRule.Predicate: ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)type" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "Microsoft\.Sql/servers" ] ] and not pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)resources" and value is [ ConfigArray: items contains [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)type" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)auditingSettings" ] ] and pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)properties" and value is [ ConfigMap : pairs contains [ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)state" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)enabled" ] ]* and pairs contains [ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)auditActionsAndGroups" and value is [ ConfigArray: items contains [ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)SUCCESSFUL_DATABASE_AUTHENTICATION_GROUP" ] and items contains [ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)FAILED_DATABASE_AUTHENTICATION_GROUP" ] and items contains [ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)BATCH_COMPLETED_GROUP" ] ]* ]* ]* ]* ]* ]* ]*

StructuralRule.Notes: This rule needed to match different date values for the apiVersion of the template because the IP restriction field was added gradually over 3 phases. * First phase was 2018-08-01 and before which is the unsupported phase - any template on a version of this resource below this us out dated and vulnerable * Second phase was 2019-06-01 and before which is the initial support and where the field was named apiServerAuthorizedIPRanges * Third and most recent phase began after 2019-06-01 and has not changed since To capture this without date comparisons we had to use the list of dates for the resource found here: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/templates/microsoft.containerservice/allversions The rule below does a search to see if the template falls in phase 1 by checking for the out-dated apiversions - flagging an issues It then checks whether it uses phase 2 apiVersions but not the appropriate field - flagging an issue It then checks whether it uses phase 3 apiVersions upto the most recent one at the time of writing for this rule (which happens to be 2021-08-01) but not the appropriate field - flagging an issue It finally then assumes that the most recent version of the fields will be maintained by Microsoft thereafter, and so we check that the apiVersion is none of the ones we've seen thus far and that it has continued to use the most recent version's field
StructuralRule.Predicate: ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)type" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)Microsoft\.ContainerService/managedClusters" ] ]* and ( (pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)apiVersion" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "2018\-08\-01\-preview|2018\-03\-31|2017\-08\-31"] ]* ) or (pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)apiVersion" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "2019\-02\-01|2019\-04\-01|2019\-06\-01"]* ] and not pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)properties" and value is [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)apiServerAuthorizedIPRanges" and value is [ ConfigArray : items contains [ ConfigConcrete: value matches ".+" ] ] ] ] ] ) or (pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)apiVersion" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "2021\-08\-01|2021\-07\-01|2021\-05\-01|2021\-03\-01|2021\-02\-01|2020\-12\-01|2020\-11\-01|2020\-09\-01|2020\-07\-01|2020\-06\-01|2020\-04\-01|2020\-03\-01|2020\-02\-01|2020\-01\-01|2019\-11\-01|2019\-10\-01|2019\-08\-01"]* ] and not pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)properties" and value is [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)apiServerAccessProfile" and value is [ ConfigMap : pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)authorizedIPRanges" and value is [ ConfigArray : items contains [ ConfigConcrete: value matches ".+" ] ] ] ] ] ] ] ) or (pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)apiVersion" and not value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "2018\-08\-01\-preview|2018\-03\-31|2017\-08\-31|2021\-08\-01|2021\-07\-01|2021\-05\-01|2021\-03\-01|2021\-02\-01|2020\-12\-01|2020\-11\-01|2020\-09\-01|2020\-07\-01|2020\-06\-01|2020\-04\-01|2020\-03\-01|2020\-02\-01|2020\-01\-01|2019\-11\-01|2019\-10\-01|2019\-08\-01|2019\-02\-01|2019\-04\-01|2019\-06\-01"] ]* and not pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)properties" and value is [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)apiServerAccessProfile" and value is [ ConfigMap : pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)authorizedIPRanges" and value is [ ConfigArray : items contains [ ConfigConcrete: value matches ".+" ] ] ] ] ] ] ] ) )

StructuralRule.Notes:
The notificationsByRole field cannot be found in any of the schema documents and almost nowhere in the Microsoft documentation except here https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/templates/microsoft.security/2020-01-01-preview/securitycontacts?tabs=json . Opensource scanners are checking for this property.
notificationsByRole defines whether to send the alerts by role or not, which is not directly related to the title of this rule's vulnerability.
When better documentation of this property is found, a new rule ought to be written to cover this factor with title: Insufficient Monitoring: Missing Security Alert Notification Personnel Roles
StructuralRule.Predicate: ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)type" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)Microsoft\.Security/securityContacts" ] ] and not pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)properties" and value is [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)alertNotifications" and value is [ ConfigMap : pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)state" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "(?i)on" ] ] ] ] ] ]

StructuralRule.Notes: This rule will only highlight lower retentionDays configured and the lack of the field being configured in an audittingsettings block. This makes for a lot less noise, since if the audittingsettings block is missing this is an indicator of a lack of auditing altogether and is highlighted by a different rule. retentiondays set to 0 is an indefinite retention period as per the documentation below.
StructuralRule.Predicate: ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)type" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "databases|Microsoft\.Sql/servers|Microsoft\.Sql/servers/databases" ] ] and (pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)resources" and value is [ ConfigArray: items contains [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)type" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "auditingSettings|Microsoft\.Sql/servers/auditingSettings|Microsoft\.Sql/servers/databases/auditingSettings" ] ] and pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)properties" and value is [ ConfigMap : pairs contains [ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)retentionDays" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value is [Number: < 90] and value is [Number: > 0] ] ]* ]* ]* ]* ]* ]* or pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)resources" and value is [ ConfigArray: items contains [ ConfigMap: pairs contains [ ConfigPair : name matches "(?i)type" and value is [ ConfigConcrete: value matches "auditingSettings|Microsoft\.Sql/servers/auditingSettings|Microsoft\.Sql/servers/databases/auditingSettings" ] ] and pairs contains [ ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)properties" and value is [ ConfigMap : not pairs contains [ConfigPair: name matches "(?i)retentionDays" ] ]* ]* ]* ]* ]*)

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Azure storage account with improper network access.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Azure storage account with improper network access.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Loose access configurations unnecessarily expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are subjected to almost continuous scanning and probing by malicious entities.
Description.Recommendations: Configure Azure Storage to block all access by default and specify the particular sources of trusted communication.

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Azure ARM Misconfiguration: Improper Storage Network Access Control

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Ansible task defines an AWS CloudTrail with logging disabled.<AltParagraph>An Ansible task defines an AWS CloudTrail with logging disabled.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, CloudTrail records events and delivers log files but logging is deliberately disabled. This can allow malicious behavior to go undetected and inhibit forensic analysis in the event of a breach. Example 1: The following Ansible task sets up a CloudTrail with logging disabled because enable_logging is set to false. 
- name: create a single region cloudtrail
  community.aws.cloudtrail:
    s3_bucket_name: mylogbucket
    s3_key_prefix: cloudtrail
    region: us-west-2
    enable_logging: false
Description.Recommendations:
Enable CloudTrail logging. Do not rely on the default parameter value, which might change. Example 2: The following Ansible task enables CloudTrail logging by setting enable_logging to true. 
- name: create a single region cloudtrail
  community.aws.cloudtrail:
    s3_bucket_name: mylogbucket
    s3_key_prefix: cloudtrail
    region: us-west-2
    enable_logging: true

Reference.Title: community.aws.cloudtrail – manage CloudTrail create, delete, update
Reference.Author: Ansible project contributors

Reference.Title: Security best practices in AWS CloudTrail
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS Ansible Misconfiguration: Insufficient CloudTrail Logging

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a CloudTrail that is not enabled for all regions.<AltParagraph>The template defines a CloudTrail that is not enabled for all regions.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, a trail logs events only in the AWS Region where it was created.
This allows unaudited and unmonitored activities to take place on the organization's AWS infrastructure.
For example, an authorized AWS user might make configurational changes that cause harm to the organization and avoid detection.
Description.Recommendations:
Create one trail that logs all management events across all AWS regions.
You can then create additional trails to log specific types of events across all regions.

Reference.Title: Security at Scale: Logging in AWS
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Insufficient CloudTrail Logging

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the access key rotation period defined by this template is too long.<AltParagraph>The access key rotation period defined by this template is too long.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Access keys with long validity periods are prone to theft and consequently place the organization at risk of breach.
Description.Recommendations: Ensure that access keys are rotated within 90 days. Rotating access keys within 90 days reduces the amount of time that a compromised access key remains in active use, consequently reducing the impact to the organization.

Reference.Title: AWS Security Blog: How to Rotate Access Keys for IAM Users
Reference.Author: Ben Brauer

Reference.Title: Best practices for managing AWS access keys
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Servcies

Reference.Title: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: Key Management Cheat Sheet
Reference.Author: Brian Russell, Drew Van Duren, Vanessa Amador, Susanna Bezold

Reference.Title: NIST Special Publication 800-57 Part 1 - Revision 5 - Recommendation for Key Management: Part 1 – General
Reference.Author: Elaine Barker

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Improper IAM Access Control Policy

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template does not implement log monitoring.<AltParagraph>The template does not implement log monitoring.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: The template does not forward audit logs to Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring. This can allow malicious behavior to go undetected and lead to delayed incident response.
Description.Recommendations: Configure the template to export audit logs to Amazon CloudWatch.

Reference.Title: Security best practices in AWS CloudTrail
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Reference.Title: Publishing Neptune Logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Reference.Title: Using Audit Logs with Amazon Neptune Clusters
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Reference.Title: Logging and Monitoring in Amazon DocumentDB
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Insufficient CloudTrail Logging

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an overly permissive IAM policy.<AltParagraph>The template defines an overly permissive IAM policy.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: IAM policies allowing unrestricted access to resources place an organization at risk. Poorly structured policies undermine the ability of an organization to control and manage changes to resources.
Description.Recommendations: When creating IAM policies, it is important to apply the least privilege principle. Architect your systems to define clear User Roles, Resources, or Assets that support your organization and Actions that users with specific roles can perform on those resources. Typically, this is defined in the form of an Access Control Matrix that distills and visualizes these policies for careful consideration and eventual implementation.

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Improper IAM Access Control Policy

Tips.Tip: Do not specify parameters of an IAM policy across different YAML fields. Define a single JSON-formatted policy to ensure future compatibility.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a user-bound Amazon IAM policy.<AltParagraph>The template defines a user-bound Amazon IAM policy.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
IAM policies that grant certain privileges to specific users can quickly become a maintenance challenge.
Over time, organizational policies and user roles change, causing such user-bound IAM policies to become outdated. Outdated IAM policies allow users to maintain access and privileges that are no longer valid. Without a quick and scalable approach to managing IAM policies, organizations can suffer authorization creep and violation of the least privilege principle.
Description.Recommendations:
Apply IAM policies to groups or roles instead of specific users. This allows an organization to quickly respond to new business requirements.
It also simplifies reassignment of privileges to users when they change roles.

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Improper IAM Access Control Policy

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Amazon DocumentDB cluster without audit logging.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Amazon DocumentDB cluster without audit logging.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Amazon DocumentDB clusters do not capture audit logs. This can allow malicious behavior to go undetected and inhibit forensic analysis in the event of a breach. Example 1: The following example template defines an Amazon DocumentDB cluster without audit logging. 
Resources:
  DocDBParameterGroup001:
    Type: AWS::DocDB::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Description: docdb cluster test group
      Family: docdb4.0
      Name: test
      Parameters:
        audit_logs: "disabled"
Description.Recommendations:
To enable Amazon DocumentDB audit logging, define and set the audit_logs parameter in your Parameters block to enabled. Example 2: The following fixes the temple in Example 1 by enabling audit logging. 
Resources:
  DocDBParameterGroup001:
    Type: AWS::DocDB::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Description: docdb cluster test group
      Family: docdb4.0
      Name: test
      Parameters:
        audit_logs: "enabled"

Reference.Title: Logging and Monitoring in Amazon DocumentDB
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Insufficient DocumentDB Logging

Description.Explanation:
By default, Amazon Neptune clusters do not capture audit logs. This can allow malicious behavior to go undetected and inhibit forensic analysis in the event of a breach. Example 1: The following example shows a configuration that defines an AWS::Neptune::DBClusterParameterGroup resource with neptune_enable_audit_log set to the insecure value 0. 
Resources:
  NeptuneParameterGroup001:
    Type: AWS::Neptune::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Description: neptune cluster test group
      Name: test
      Parameters:
        neptune_enable_audit_log: 0
Example 2: The following example shows a configuration that defines an AWS::Neptune::DBClusterParameterGroup resource with neptune_enable_audit_log unset. 
Resources:
  NeptuneParameterGroup001:
    Type: AWS::Neptune::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Description: neptune cluster test group
      Name: test
      Parameters:
        # MISSING neptune_enable_audit_log ...
Description.Recommendations:
To enable Amazon Neptune audit logging, define and set the neptune_enable_audit_log parameter in your Parameters block. Example 3: The following fixes the problem in Example 1 by enabling audit logging. 
Resources:
  NeptuneParameterGroup001:
    Type: AWS::Neptune::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Description: neptune cluster test group
      Name: test
      Parameters:
        neptune_enable_audit_log: 1

Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Reference.Title: Logging and Monitoring Amazon Neptune Resources
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Ansible task defines a CloudWatch Log Group with no retention period.<AltParagraph>An Ansible task defines a CloudWatch Log Group with no retention period.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, CloudWatch Log Groups retain logs indefinitely. An unset retention value indicates that organizational data handling policies have not been consulted in order to set appropriate configurations. This might result in unnecessary expenses for the organization to store and manage logging events. An attacker can launch a Denial of Wallet (DoW) attack by persistently prompting spurious event-logging over an extended period of time, which can impact the organization financially. Example 1: The following example shows an Ansible task that fails to define a retention policy. 
- name: create a log_group in CloudWatchLogs
  community.aws.cloudwatchlogs_log_group:
    log_group_name: test-log-group
    tags: { "Name": "test-log-group", "Env" : "QA" }
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure that CloudWatch Log Groups are configured with an appropriate retention period. It is important to understand and follow organizational data and log management policies in order to reduce any financial overhead and any other related liabilities associated with storing and managing log data. Example 2: The following Ansible task defines a retention policy of 100 days. 
- name: create log_group in CloudWatchLogs
  community.aws.cloudwatchlogs_log_group:
    log_group_name: test-log-group
    tags: { "Name": "test-log-group", "Env" : "QA" }
    retention: 100

Reference.Title: community.aws.cloudwatchlogs_log_group – create or delete log_group in CloudWatchLogs

Reference.Author: AWS

Reference.Author: Daniel Kelly, Frank G.Glavin, Enda Barrett

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Ansible task creates an Amazon EC2 image (AMI) and attaches a block device without data at rest encryption to the AMI.<AltParagraph>An Ansible task creates an Amazon EC2 image (AMI) and attaches a block device without data at rest encryption to the AMI.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
An Amazon EC2 AMI that maps an unencrypted block device exposes the data to unauthorized access and potential theft. Example 1: The following Ansible task creates an Amazon EC2 AMI and attaches a block device without data at rest encryption to the AMI because the encrypted parameter is set to false. 
- name: Basic AMI Creation
  amazon.aws.ec2_ami:
    state: present
    instance_id: i-xxxxxx
    name: test_ami
    device_mapping:
      device_name: /dev/sda
      encrypted: false
Description.Recommendations:
Attach only encrypted block devices to an Amazon EC2 AMI to protect the data at rest. Amazon encrypted block devices use the industry standard AES-256 encryption algorithm to encrypt data on the server. Do not rely on the default parameter value, which might change. Example 2: The following Ansible task creates an Amazon EC2 AMI and attaches a block device with data at rest encryption to the AMI by setting the encrypted parameter to true. 
- name: Basic AMI Creation
  amazon.aws.ec2_ami:
    state: present
    instance_id: i-xxxxxx
    name: test_ami
    device_mapping:
      device_name: /dev/sda
      encrypted: true

Reference.Title: amazon.aws.ec2_ami – Create or destroy an image (AMI) in ec2
Reference.Author: Duffield et al.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Ansible task creates an Amazon Kinesis data stream without data at rest encryption.<AltParagraph>An Ansible task creates an Amazon Kinesis data stream without data at rest encryption.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
An unencrypted Amazon Kinesis stream storage layer exposes the data to unauthorized access and potential theft. Example 1: The following Ansible task sets up a Kinesis stream without data at rest encryption because the encryption_state parameter is set to disabled. 
- name: Set up Kinesis Stream with 10 shards and wait for the stream to become active
  community.aws.kinesis_stream:
    name: test-stream
    shards: 10
    wait: yes
    wait_timeout: 600
    encryption_state: disabled
  register: test_stream
Description.Recommendations:
Enable server-side encryption so data is encrypted at rest within the Kinesis Data Streams service. Kinesis server-side encryption uses the industry standard AES-256 encryption algorithm to encrypt data on the server. Do not rely on the default parameter value, which might change. Example 2: The following Ansible task creates a Kinesis stream with data at rest encryption by setting the encryption_state parameter to enabled and the encryption_type parameter to KMS. The key_id parameter specifies the AWS KMS key used to encrypt and decrypt data. 
- name: Set up Kinesis Stream with 10 shards and wait for the stream to become active
  community.aws.kinesis_stream:
    name: test-stream
    shards: 10
    wait: yes
    wait_timeout: 600
    encryption_state: enabled
    encryption_type: KMS
    key_id: alias/foobar/kinesis
  register: test_stream

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Ansible task creates an Amazon EFS file system without data at rest encryption.<AltParagraph>An Ansible task defines an Amazon EFS file system without data at rest encryption.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, an EFS file system is not encrypted. This exposes the data to unauthorized access and potential theft. Example 1: The following Ansible task sets up an EFS file system without data at rest encryption because the encrypt parameter is set to no. 
- name: EFS provisioning
  community.aws.efs:
    state: present
    name: myTestEFS
    encrypt: no
    targets:
      - subnet_id: subnet-12345678
        security_groups: [ "sg-87654321" ]
Description.Recommendations:
Enable EFS encryption to protect the data at rest. Amazon EFS encryption uses the industry standard AES-256 encryption algorithm to encrypt data on the server. Do not rely on the default parameter value, which might change. Example 2: The following Ansible task creates an encrypted EFS file system by setting the encrypt parameter to yes. 
- name: EFS provisioning
  community.aws.efs:
    state: present
    name: myTestEFS
    encrypt: yes
    targets:
      - subnet_id: subnet-12345678
        security_groups: [ "sg-87654321" ]

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Ansible task defines a wildcard lambda principal.<AltParagraph>An Ansible task defines a wildcard lambda principal.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
A wildcard configuration for lambda principals violates the least privilege principle and allows an attacker to invoke the lambda from any account. Example 1: The following example Ansible task defines a wildcard lambda principal. 
- name: Create Lambda policy statement for S3 event notification
  community.aws.lambda_policy:
    action: lambda:InvokeFunction
    function_name: functionName
    principal: *
    statement_id: lambda-s3-demobucket-access-log
    source_arn: arn:aws:s3:us-west-2:123456789012:demobucket
    source_account: 123456789012
    state: present
Description.Recommendations:
Explicitly define lambda principals to restrict invocation of the lambda function to authorized accounts and services. Example 2: The following example Ansible task defines a specific principal authorized to invoke the lambda. 
- name: Create Lambda policy statement for S3 event notification
  community.aws.lambda_policy:
    action: lambda:InvokeFunction
    function_name: functionName
    principal: s3.amazonaws.com
    statement_id: lambda-s3-demobucket-access-log
    source_arn: arn:aws:s3:us-west-2:123456789012:demobucket
    source_account: 123456789012
    state: present

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Ansible task defines an Azure App Service that does not enforce HTTPS communication.<AltParagraph>The Ansible task defines an Azure App Service that does not enforce HTTPS communication.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Unencrypted communication channels are prone to eavesdropping and tampering. Serving web applications over HTTP allows attackers to perform man-in-the-middle attacks, giving them access to read or modify the data in transit over the channel. Example 1: The following example shows an Ansible task that defines an Azure App Service that does not enforce HTTPS communication. 
- name: app service
  azure_rm_webapp:
    resource_group: testGroup
    name: testApp
    https_only: false
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Enforce transport encryption to ensure that all data exchange is performed over encrypted channels and inhibit man-in-the-middle attacks. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It enforces HTTPS communication by enabling the https_only property. 
- name: app service
  azure_rm_webapp:
    resource_group: testGroup
    name: testApp
    https_only: true
    ...

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Ansible task defines an AKS cluster that does not send log events to Azure Monitor.<AltParagraph>The Ansible task defines an AKS cluster that does not send log events to Azure Monitor.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) clusters created by Ansible do not send log events to Azure Monitor. This can allow malicious behavior to go undetected and prevent forensic analysis in the event of a breach. Example 1: The following example Ansible task shows an AKS cluster that does not send log events to Azure Monitor. 
- name: AKS Instance
  azure_rm_aks:
    name:
    resource_group: testResourceGroup
    location: eastus
    ...
    addon:
      monitoring:
        log_analytics_workspace_resource_id: logws001
        enabled: no
Description.Recommendations:
To make Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) clusters send log events to Azure Monitor, enable the log analytics agent using the addon.monitoring parameter. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines the required addon.monitoring.enabled parameter and sets it to yes. 
 - name: AKS Instance
  azure_rm_aks:
    name:
    resource_group: testResourceGroup
    location: eastus
    ...
    addon:
      monitoring:
        log_analytics_workspace_resource_id: logws001
        enabled: yes

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Ansible task defines an Azure storage account with unrestricted network access.<AltParagraph>The Ansible task defines an Azure storage account with unrestricted network access.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Azure storage accounts created by Ansible accept connections from clients on any network. Loose access configurations unnecessarily expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are subjected to almost continuous scanning and probing by malicious entities. Example 1: The following example Ansible task fails to restrict network access to an Azure storage account. 
- name: storage with network acl
azure_rm_storageaccount:
  resource_group: testGroup
  name: sa001
  type: Standard_RAGRS
  network_acls:
    bypass: AzureServices,Metrics
    default_action: Deny
    ip_rules:
      - value: 0.0.0.0/0
        action: Allow
Description.Recommendations:
Restrict critical services access to specific IP addresses, ranges, or virtual networks. Configure Azure Storage firewall rules to block all traffic by default and specify the particular sources of trusted communication. To specify trusted sources, configure the network_acls parameter using ip_rules or virtual_network_rules. Then, to block all traffic by default, configure the default_action parameter to Deny. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It restricts network access to an Azure storage account to a specific virtual network, a specific IP address and subnet. 
- name: storage with network acl
azure_rm_storageaccount:
  resource_group: testGroup
  name: sa001
  type: Standard_RAGRS
  network_acls:
    bypass: AzureServices,Metrics
    default_action: Deny
    virtual_network_rules:
      - id: /subscriptions/mySubscriptionId/resourceGroups/myResourceGroup/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/myVnet/subnets/mySubnet
        action: Allow
    ip_rules:
      - value: 1.2.3.4
        action: Allow
      - value: 123.234.123.0/24
        action: Allow

Reference.Author: Microsoft

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Ansible task defines an Azure Monitor log profile that does not collect all Activity log administrative events.<AltParagraph>The Ansible task defines an Azure Monitor log profile that does not collect all Activity log administrative events.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: A lack of audit records limits the ability to detect and respond to security related incidents and prevents forensic investigation.
Description.Recommendations: Configure Azure Monitor to collect logs for all Activity log administrative category events. Activity log administrative category events include information on the creation, modification, and the start of resources. Specifically, include the Write, Delete, and Action categories.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Ansible task explicitly disables transport encryption for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL.<AltParagraph>The Ansible task explicitly disables transport encryption for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Ansible tasks do not enable Azure Database for PostgreSQL transport encryption (as per Azure.Azcollection v1.11.0 and earlier). Unencrypted communication channels are prone to eavesdropping and tampering. Disabling transport security exposes the data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering. Example 1: The following example Ansible task defines an Azure Database for PostgreSQL with transport encryption disabled. 
- name: Create Postgres Server
  azure.azcollection.azure_rm_postgresqlserver:
    resource_group: testGroup
    name: testPostgres
    sku:
      name: B_Gen5_1
      tier: Basic
    location: westeurope
    storage_mb: 8096
    version: 5.6
    enforce_ssl: false
    admin_username: test
    admin_password: complicatedPass
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure that transport encryption is not disabled for Azure Database for PostgreSQL to protect data in transit. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It explicitly enables transport encryption. 
- name: Create Postgres Server
  azure.azcollection.azure_rm_postgresqlserver:
    resource_group: testGroup
    name: testPostgres
    sku:
      name: B_Gen5_1
      tier: Basic
    location: westeurope
    storage_mb: 8096
    enforce_ssl: true
    version: 5.6
    admin_username: test
    admin_password: complicatedPass

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Ansible task defines an Azure Blob Storage container that allows anonymous access.<AltParagraph>The Ansible task defines an Azure Blob Storage container that allows anonymous access.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Azure Blob Storage containers prevent anonymous access to their Blobs. Insufficient access configurations expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Resources open to public access might unintentionally leak sensitive data. Example 1: The following example Ansible task defines an Azure Blob Storage container with the public_access parameter set to container. This allows anonymous access to all of the Container's blobs and data. 
- name: Create container test
  azure_rm_storageblob:
    resource_group: testGroup
    storage_account_name: sa001
    container: testContainer
    ...
    public_access: container
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Restrict access to Azure Blob Storage containers that store confidential data to authorized users. Review your organization's data handling policies when creating resources that are readable by anonymous users. When making a change to access restrictions, identify all dependent systems to limit potential disruptions. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines an Azure Blob Storage container that does not allow public access by omitting the public_access parameter. 
- name: Create container test
  azure_rm_storageblob:
    resource_group: testGroup
    storage_account_name: sa001
    container: testContainer
    ...

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Ansible task defines a network security group that allows access to administrative services.<AltParagraph>The Ansible task defines a network security group that allows access to administrative services.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Overly broad configurations expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are subjected to almost continuous scanning and probing by attackers. This is especially problematic when a zero-day exploit for an exposed service is discovered and published (e.g. Heartbleed). Attackers can actively pursue and search for unpatched and exposed systems to exploit. Example 1: The following example Ansible task allows unrestricted inbound traffic to a range of ports, including the RDP service port (3389). 
- name: testFWRule
azure_rm_securitygroup:
    resource_group: testRG
    name: test
    rules:
    - name: rule001
        priority: 100
        direction: Inbound
        access: Allow
        protocol: "*"
        source_port_range: "*"
        destination_port_range: "3388-3398"
        source_address_prefix: "*"
        destination_address_prefix: "*"
    - name: rule002
        priority: 100
        direction: Inbound
        access: Allow
        protocol: "*"
        source_port_range: "*"
        destination_port_range: 22
        source_address_prefix: "*"
        destination_address_prefix: "*"
Description.Recommendations:
Define Azure Network Security Groups to restrict access to services and make those services only available to as limited an audience as possible. For example, do not make ports that are typically used for management activities of services publicly accessible. Make sure these ports are only available to a restricted pool of systems that require authorized access. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1 by restricting the range of IP addresses that may connect to the RDP service (3389). 
    - name: testFWRule
    azure_rm_securitygroup:
        resource_group: testRG
        name: test
        rules:
        - name: rule001
            priority: 100
            direction: Inbound
            access: Allow
            protocol: "*"
            source_port_range: "*"
            destination_port_range: "3388-3398"
            source_address_prefix: "152.234.123.1"
            destination_address_prefix: "*"
        - name: rule002
            priority: 100
            direction: Inbound
            access: Allow
            protocol: "*"
            source_port_range: "*"
            destination_port_range: 22
            source_address_prefix: "152.234.123.1"
            destination_address_prefix: "*"

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Ansible task defines a storage account that does not enforce encryption in transit.<AltParagraph>The Anisble task defines a storage account that does not enforce encryption in transit.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Unencrypted communication channels are prone to eavesdropping and tampering. By default, the https_only setting is set to yes enforcing secure transfer for an Azure storage account. However, this setting can be explicitly disabled. Disabling secure transfer exposes the stored data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering. Example 1: The following Ansible task shows a storage account that does not enforce secure transfer. 
- name: create a storage account
  azure_rm_storageaccount:
    resource_group: testResGroup
    name: sa0001
    type: Standard_GRS
    https_only: no
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure that Azure storage accounts require secure connections from clients by setting https_only to yes. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It explicitly configures the Azure storage account to only accept requests over a secure channel. 
- name: create a storage account
  azure_rm_storageaccount:
    resource_group: testResGroup
    name: sa0001
    type: Standard_GRS
    https_only: yes

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the command to start the Kubernetes API server does not enable the PodSecurityPolicy admission controller.<AltParagraph>The command to start a Kubernetes API server does not enable the PodSecurityPolicy admission controller.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
The lack of a PodSecurityPolicy admission controller is indicative of weak security controls unless there is an alternative policy enforcement tool for Kubernetes such as K-Rail, Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper. The PodSecurityPolicy admission controller enforces Pod security policies that specify permissible security-related Pod attributes in a cluster. For instance, using PodSecurityPolicy, you can forbid privileged containers and disallow privilege escalation by default whenever a Pod is created. Example 1: The following Pod definition starts a Kubernetes API server without enabling the PodSecurityPolicy admission controller. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Unless there is an alternative policy enforcement tool in place for the Kubernetes API server, in the command to start a Kubernetes API server, add PodSecurityPolicy to the admission controllers listed in the --enable-admission-plugins flag. Example 2: The following Pod definition starts a Kubernetes API server with the PodSecurityPolicy admission controller. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=PodSecurityPolicy,NodeRestriction
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing PodSecurityPolicy Admission Controller

Tips.Tip: Enabling the PodSecurityPolicy admission controller alone does not improve security posture. Appropriate Pod security policies must be written so the admission controller can enforce the desired security requirements.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Kubelet configuration prevents the Kubelet from configuring iptables.<AltParagraph>The Kubelet configuration prevents the Kubelet from configuring iptables.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Kubelets automatically make the required changes to iptables based on the networking options in Pod configurations. Setting makeIPTablesUtilChains to enabled:false in a Kubelet configuration prevents the Kubelet from managing network traffic between containers and the rest of the world. This prevents the Kubelet from enforcing the necessary network security requirements and setting up the connectivity requested by containers. Example 1: The following Kubelet configuration prevents a Kubelet from making the required changes to iptables because of the setting makeIPTablesUtilChains: false. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
makeIPTablesUtilChains: false
Description.Recommendations:
Allow Kubelets to automatically make required changes to iptables. Example 2: The following Kubelet configuration allows a Kubelet to make the required changes to iptables because of the setting makeIPTablesUtilChains: true. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
makeIPTablesUtilChains: true

Reference.Title: Set Kubelet parameters via a config file
Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Automated iptables Management Disabled

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Kubelet configuration allows a Kubelet to override kernel defaults.<AltParagraph>The Kubelet configuration allows a Kubelet to override kernel defaults.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
If the ProtectKernelDefaults setting is left unset or is set to false, a Kubelet can modify kernel parameters at runtime. Kernel parameters should be optimized and hardened before the Kubernetes deployment. Granting a Kubelet the ability to alter kernel parameters expands the attack surface of the host operating system. Example 1: The following Kubelet configuration permits a Kubelet to configure kernel parameters because of the ProtectKernelDefaults: false setting. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
ProtectKernelDefaults: false
Description.Recommendations:
Do not allow any Kubelet to configure kernel parameters. Example 2: The following Kubelet configuration prevents a Kubelet from configuring kernel parameters because of the ProtectKernelDefaults: true setting. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
ProtectKernelDefaults: true

Reference.Title: Set Kubelet parameters via a config file
Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Kernel Defaults Overridden

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the command to start the Kubernetes API server disables the ServiceAccount admission controller.<AltParagraph>The command to start a Kubernetes API server disables the ServiceAccount admission controller.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Kubernetes distinguishes between the concept of a user account and a service account, which is for a process to run in a Pod. The ServiceAccount admission controller automates the service account management. Some benefits of the ServiceAccount admission controller are to mitigate access token exfiltration with automated credential rotation and eliminate the need to persist secrets in storage. The ServiceAccount admission controller is enabled by default but has been deliberately disabled. Example 1: The following Pod definition starts a Kubernetes API server and disables the ServiceAccount admission controller. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --disable-admission-plugins=ServiceAccount,PodNodeSelector
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, remove ServiceAccount from the list of admission controllers specified in the --disable-admission-plugins flag. Example 2: The following Pod definition starts a Kubernetes API server without disabling the ServiceAccount admission controller. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --disable-admission-plugins=PodNodeSelector
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing ServiceAccount Admission Controller

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the command to start the Kubernetes controller manager permits the sharing of service account credentials among controllers.<AltParagraph>The command to start the Kubernetes controller manager permits service account credentials shared among controllers.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Service account credentials are shared among controllers because the command to start the Kubernetes controller manager does not contain the --use-service-account-credentials=true flag. This flag instructs the controller manager to start each controller using a separate service account. When used in combination with role-based access control (RBAC), this ensures that each controller runs with the minimum permissions needed to perform its tasks. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager without the --use-service-account-credentials flag. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
        - /usr/local/bin/kube-controller-manager
    image: k8s.gcr.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.9.7
...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes controller manager, instruct the controller manager to start each controller using a separate service account. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager with the --use-service-account-credentials=true flag. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
        - /usr/local/bin/kube-controller-manager
        - --use-service-account-credentials=true
    image: k8s.gcr.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.9.7
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Shared Service Account Credentials

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the private key for signing service account tokens is unspecified.<AltParagraph>The private key for signing service account tokens is unspecified.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes API server can authenticate API requests by service account tokens. Such tokens are generated and signed by the Kubernetes token controller. Use the --service-account-private-key-file flag to specify the token signing key. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager without the --service-account-private-key-file flag. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
        - kube-controller-manager
    image: k8s.gcr.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.9.7
...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes controller manager, specify the key for signing service account tokens. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager and specifies the token signing key with the --service-account-private-key-file flag. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
        - kube-controller-manager
        - --service-account-private-key-file=foobar.pem
    image: k8s.gcr.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.9.7
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing Service Account Token Authentication

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, Kubelet uses a self-signed certificate for TLS connections in the absence of an x509 certificate definition.<AltParagraph>Kubelet uses a self-signed certificate for TLS connections in the absence of an x509 certificate definition.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
The tlsCertFile and tlsPrivateKeyFile fields in a Kubelet configuration define the x509 certificate used to serve HTTPS. By failing to provide both of them, a self-signed certificate and key are generated for the public address, which is susceptible to a man-in-the-middle attack. Example 1: The following Kubelet configuration does not specify the tlsCertFile and tlsPrivateKeyFile fields so the Kubelet automatically generates a self-signed certificate for TLS connections. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
Description.Recommendations:
Provide a certificate and a matching private key to the Kubelet server to set up TLS connections. Example 2: The following Kubelet configuration specifies the location of the certificate and the private key to set up TLS connections in the tlsCertFile and tlsPrivateKeyFile fields respectively. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
tlsCertFile: foobar.crt
tlsPrivateKeyFile: foobar.pem

Reference.Title: Set Kubelet parameters via a config file
Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Weak SSL Certificate for Kubelet

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the command to start the Kubernetes API server does not enable the NodeRestriction admission controller.<AltParagraph>The command to start a Kubernetes API server does not enable the NodeRestriction admission controller.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Always enable the NodeRestriction admission controller for a Kubernetes API server. The NodeRestriction admission controller limits every Kubelet to modify its Node and Pod objects as well as deny access to sensitive system objects. This prevents any compromised node from gaining privileges on other nodes of a Kubernetes cluster. Example 1: The following Pod definition starts a Kubernetes API server without enabling the NodeRestriction admission controller. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=PodSecurityPolicy
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, add NodeRestriction to the list of admission controllers specified in the --enable-admission-plugins flag. Example 2: The following Pod definition starts a Kubernetes API server with the NodeRestriction admission controller. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurityPolicy
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing NodeRestriction Admission Controller

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the command to start an etcd instance does not enable TLS for client-server communication.<AltParagraph>The command to start an etcd instance does not enable TLS for client-server communication.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Kubernetes keeps sensitive data in an etcd cluster. Every etcd instance must serve clients over TLS connections but the command-line flags for setting up the TLS connections are missing. Example 1: The following configuration starts an etcd instance without specifying both the --cert-file and --key-file flags for setting up TLS connections. 
apiVersion: v1
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - etcd
      - --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd
    image: k8s.gcr.io/etcd:3.4.3-0
  ...
Description.Recommendations:
Enable TLS client-to-server connections when starting an etcd instance. Example 2: The following configuration starts an etcd instance and provides both the --cert-file and --key-file flags for setting up TLS connections. 
apiVersion: v1
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - etcd
	  - --cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt
	  - --key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
    image: k8s.gcr.io/etcd:3.4.3-0
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Insecure etcd Client Transport

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the idle timeout of the streaming connection is disabled.<AltParagraph>The idle timeout of the streaming connection is disabled.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
The streamingConnectionIdleTimeout field of a Kubelet configuration specifies the maximum amount of time a streaming connection is idle before the connection is automatically closed. Setting idle timeouts protects against denial-of-service attacks and running out of connections. Setting the field value to 0 disables the idle timeout. Example 1: The following Kubelet configuration disables the streaming connection timeout by setting the streamingConnectionIdleTimeout field to 0. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
streamingConnectionIdleTimeout: 0
Description.Recommendations:
By default, the idle timeout for the streaming connection is not disabled. The disablement suggests that a software component may rely on long-live connections to function. Before applying an appropriate non-zero idle timeout, make sure all impacted components can handle timeouts gracefully. Do not rely on the default value, which might change and be too high for many environments. Example 2: The following Kubelet configuration enables the streaming connection timeout by setting the streamingConnectionIdleTimeout field to 5m (5 minutes). 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
streamingConnectionIdleTimeout: 5m

Reference.Title: Set Kubelet parameters via a config file
Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Kubelet Streaming Connection Timeout Disabled

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, X509 client certificate authentication to the Kubelet's HTTPS endpoint is not defined.<AltParagraph>X509 client certificate authentication to the Kubelet's HTTPS endpoint is not defined.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Kubelets can authenticate clients but the Certificate Authority (CA) bundle used to verify the client certificate is not defined in the Kubelet Configuration. Because Kubelets are the Kubernetes principal agents used to manage a worker machine workload, attackers can use anonymous requests to gain access to insufficiently protected and security-sensitive service APIs. Example 1: The following Kubelet configuration does not contain the clientCAFile field that specifies the CA bundle used to verify client certificates. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
Description.Recommendations:
Prevent anonymous requests to the Kubelet server and define a CA bundle for certificate-based client authentication. Example 2: The following Kubelet configuration prevents anonymous requests by setting anonymous to enabled:false and defines a CA bundle for certificate-based client authentications in the clientCAFile field. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false
  x509:
    clientCAFile: foobar.pem

Reference.Title: Set Kubelet parameters via a config file
Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing Kubelet Certificate Authentication

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Container lacks security context.<AltParagraph>A Container lacks security context.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
It is good practice to define permissions on a granular basis that adhere to the Least Privilege Principle. A Kubernetes security context defines privileges and access control settings for a Container or Pod. A Container lacks security context if there is no such setting at both the Pod and Container level. Example 1: The following configuration defines a Pod without any security context because there is no securityContext field. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx
      ports:
        - name: web
          containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
Description.Recommendations:
Always configure an appropriate security context for a Container or Pod. Example 2: The following configuration contains a securityContext field for both the Pod and the Container. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 3000
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx
      ports:
        - name: web
          containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false

Reference.Title: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container
Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing Security Context

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the command to start an etcd instance does not enable a TLS connection between peers.<AltParagraph>The command to start an etcd instance does not enable a TLS connection between peers.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Kubernetes keeps sensitive data in an etcd cluster. Every etcd instance in a cluster should always communicate with peers over a TLS connection but the command-line flags for setting up the TLS connection are missing. Example 1: The following configuration starts an etcd instance without specifying both the --peer-cert-file and --peer-key-file flags for setting up a TLS connection. 
apiVersion: v1
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - etcd
      - --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd
    image: k8s.gcr.io/etcd:3.4.3-0
...
Description.Recommendations:
If the etcd instance is a member of an etcd cluster, enable TLS peer connections when starting the instance. Example 2: The following configuration starts an etcd instance and provides both the --peer-cert-file and --peer-key-file flags for setting up a TLS connection. 
apiVersion: v1
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - etcd
        - --peer-cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.crt
        - --peer-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.key
    image: k8s.gcr.io/etcd:3.4.3-0
...

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the command to start the Kubernetes API server does not enable the SecurityContextDeny admission controller.<AltParagraph>The command to start a Kubernetes API server does not enable the SecurityContextDeny admission controller.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
The SecurityContextDeny admission controller prevents Pods from setting certain SecurityContext fields that allow for privilege escalation in a Kubernetes cluster. Unless there is an alternative policy enforcement tool for Kubernetes, such as appropriate Pod security policies, the SecurityContextDeny admission controller should be enabled. Example 1: The following Pod definition starts a Kubernetes API server without enabling the SecurityContextDeny admission controller. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, add SecurityContextDeny to the list of admission controllers specified in the --enable-admission-plugins flag. Example 2: The following Pod definition starts a Kubernetes API server with the SecurityContextDeny admission controller. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=SecurityContextDeny,NodeRestriction
    ...

Description.Abstract: An Amazon S3 bucket is created without enabling encryption at rest.
Description.Explanation: An Amazon S3 bucket is created without server-side encryption. Encryption mitigates data breaches by making data unreadable to anyone without the proper credentials. Encryption at rest can help satisfy some industrial and government compliance requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI.
Description.Recommendations: Encryption at rest is a vital control against data breaches. Whenever you create an S3 bucket, enable encryption by default and specify a valid encryption key. Use a key automatically generated by S3 or an existing one stored in the AWS Key Management Service.

Reference.Title: GDPR Article 32
Reference.Publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union

Reference.Title: Amazon Simple Storage Service User Guide
Fortify Taxonomy | AWS Ansible Misconfiguration: Insecure S3 Bucket Storage

Tips.Tip: Changing the default encryption setting only affects objects subsequently uploaded to S3.
Even if there is a setting to encrypt objects by default when they are stored in the bucket, authorized clients can still intentionally upload unencrypted data.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Amazon EBS volume with no encryption.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Amazon EBS volume with no encryption.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, EBS volumes are not encrypted. Example 1: The following example template exposes the data to potential theft and unauthorized access. 
	Resources:
  	  EBSVOLExample:
    	Type: AWS::EC2::Volume
    	Properties:
      	  Encrypted: false
Description.Recommendations:
Fortify recommends that you enable EBS encryption to protect the data at rest. Amazon EBS encryption uses the industry standard AES-256 encryption algorithm to encrypt your data on the server that hosts your EBS volume. Example 2: The following example template enable EBS encryption to protect the data at rest. 
	Resources:
  	  EBSVOLExample:
    	Type: AWS::EC2::Volume
    	Properties:
      	  Encrypted: true

Description.Abstract: An Ansible task defines a CloudTrail log file without integrity validation.
Description.Explanation:
By default, CloudTrail log file validation is disabled, which prevents investigators from confirming that there has been no external tampering with CloudTrail log files. This enables an attacker with the necessary privileges to perform harmful configuration changes and hide them by modifying the CloudTrail logs. Example 1: The following Ansible task sets up a CloudTrail configuration without log file integrity validation because the enable_log_file_validation parameter is missing. 
- name: create a single region cloudtrail
  community.aws.cloudtrail:
    s3_bucket_name: mylogbucket
    s3_key_prefix: cloudtrail
    region: us-west-2
Description.Recommendations:
Enable CloudTrail log file validation to collect digest files, which can be used to determine if anyone has tampered with log files. Example 2: The following Ansible task defines a CloudTrail configuration and enables the log file integrity validation by setting the enable_log_file_validation parameter to yes. 
- name: create a single region cloudtrail
  community.aws.cloudtrail:
    s3_bucket_name: mylogbucket
    s3_key_prefix: cloudtrail
    region: us-west-2
    enable_log_file_validation: yes

Reference.Title: community.aws.cloudtrail – manage CloudTrail create, delete, update
Reference.Author: Ansible project contributors

Reference.Title: Security at Scale: Logging in AWS
Reference.Author: Amazon Web Services

Description.Abstract: An Ansible task defines an AWS Security Group with overly broad access permissions.
Description.Explanation:
Loose access configurations unnecessarily expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are typically subjected to near continuous scanning and probing by malicious entities. This is especially problematic when a zero-day exploit for an exposed service is discovered and published (e.g Heartbleed). Attackers can actively pursue and search for unpatched and exposed systems to exploit. Example 1: The following Ansible task defines an AWS Security Group that opens to the world (0.0.0.0/0) the TCP port 22, where an SSH server typically responds to incoming connection requests. 
- name: Task to open SSH port
  amazon.aws.ec2_group:
    name: demo_security_group
    description: Open the ssh port to the world
    state: present
    vpc_id: 123456
    region: us-west-1
    rules:
    - proto: tcp
        ports: 22
        cidr_ip: 0.0.0.0/0
Description.Recommendations:
Define AWS Security Groups that restrict access to services and ensure the services are available to as limited an audience as possible. For example, do not make ports that are typically used for service management activities publicly accessible. Ensure these ports are only available to a restricted pool of systems that require authorized access. Example 2: The following Ansible task defines an AWS Security Group that opens the TCP port 22 to a specific local IP address. 
- name: Task to open SSH port to a designated IP
  amazon.aws.ec2_group:
    name: demo_security_group
    description: Open the ssh port to an IP
    state: present
    vpc_id: 123456
    region: us-west-1
    rules:
    - proto: tcp
        ports: 22
        cidr_ip: 192.168.7.23

Description.Abstract: An Amazon S3 bucket is created without enabling all of the S3 Block Public Access settings.
Description.Explanation:
A misconfiguration of public access to an S3 bucket is a leading cause of data breaches.
Although S3 buckets block public access by default, any authorized user can update bucket policies or access control lists (ACLs) to allow public access.
Description.Recommendations: Block public access of S3 data and forbid anyone from adding policies or ACLs that grant public access.

Reference.Title: There's a Hole in that Bucket!: A Large-scale Analysis of Misconfigured S3 Buckets
Reference.Publisher: ACSAC '18: Proceedings of the 34th Annual Computer Security Applications Conference

Reference.Title: Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage
Fortify Taxonomy | AWS Ansible Misconfiguration: Improper S3 Bucket Network Access Control

Tips.Tip: The AWS Account root user who owns an S3 bucket can always update public access policies even if there is a policy to deny updates by any user.

Description.Abstract: An Ansible task enables public access to an Amazon Redshift cluster.
Description.Explanation:
Amazon Redshift clusters are by default not publicly accessible. Enabling public access to a cluster results in a wider attack surface for the organization. Example 1: The following example shows an Ansible task that explicitly enables public access to an Amazon Redshift cluster by setting the publicly_accessible parameter to yes. 
- name: example1
  community.aws.redshift:
    identifier: mycluster
    command: create
    db_name: mydb
    node_type: ds1.xlarge
    username: "{{ username }}"
    password: "{{ password }}"
    publicly_accessible: yes
Description.Recommendations:
Restrict communication with the Amazon Redshift cluster to a select pool of systems that have a legitimate need to connect to the cluster. Example 2: The following Ansible task fixes the problem in Example 1. It explicitly prevents public access to the Amazon Redshift cluster by setting the publicly_accessible parameter to no. 
- name: example2
  community.aws.redshift:
    identifier: mycluster
    command: create
    db_name: mydb
    node_type: ds1.xlarge
    username: "{{ username }}"
    password: "{{ password }}"
    publicly_accessible: no

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a logging configuration with an insufficient audit retention period.<AltParagraph>The template defines a logging configuration with an insufficient audit retention period.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: A short retention period reduces the amount of log information that the organization can consult in the event of an investigation. Industry standards recommend different retention periods depending on the type of data and the legal obligations required for the organization.
