Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Azure Monitor log profile that does not collect all Activity Log administrative events.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Azure Monitor log profile that does not collect all Activity Log administrative events.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
A lack of audit records limits the ability to detect and respond to security related incidents and prevents forensic investigation. Example 1: The following example template defines an Azure Monitor log profile that does not collect all Activity Log administrative events. 
{
    "name": "string",
    "type": "microsoft.insights/logprofiles",
    "apiVersion": "2016-03-01",
    ...
    "properties": {
        ...
        "categories": [
            "Write"
        ],
        ...
    }
}
Description.Recommendations:
Configure Azure Monitor to collect logs for all Activity Log administrative category events. Activity Log administrative category events include information on the creation, modification, and the starting of resources. Specifically, Microsoft.Insights/logprofiles should include Write,Delete, and Action categories. Log Profiles are a legacy method for collecting Activity Log events. Consider transitioning to diagnostic settings to collect the same events with better functionality and consistency. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines an Activity Monitor log profile that collects all Activity Log administrative events. 
{
    "name": "string",
    "type": "microsoft.insights/logprofiles",
    "apiVersion": "2016-03-01",
    ...
    "properties": {
        ...
        "categories": [
            "Write", "Delete", "Action"
        ],
        ...
    }
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Azure Cosmos DB with unrestricted network access.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Azure Cosmos DB with unrestricted network access.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Relaxed access configurations expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the internet are subjected to almost continuous scanning and probing by malicious entities. This is especially problematic when a zero-day exploit for an exposed service is discovered and published (e.g Heartbleed). Attackers can actively pursue and search for unpatched and exposed systems to exploit. Example 1: The following example template defines an Azure Cosmos DB with unrestricted network access. The publicNetworkAccess property is set to Enabled and the IP address range includes all IPs. 
{
    "type": "Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts",
    "apiVersion": "2021-04-15",
    ...
    "properties": {
        ...
        "publicNetworkAccess": "Enabled",
        "ipRules":[{
                "ipAddressOrRange":  "0.0.0.0"
            }]
    ...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Restrict access to services and ensure the services are available to as limited an audience as possible. For example, do not make ports that are typically used for service management activities publicly accessible. Make sure these ports are only available to a restricted pool of systems that require authorized access. Limit Azure Cosmos DB interaction to the scope of IPs that require access to the database. This allows the organization to better protect the assets stored in the database and reduce its overall surface area of attack. Ensure that the publicNetworkAccess property is set to Disabled. If the database must be accessed from a public IP range, create the necessary ipRules or ipRangeFilter to specify an allowed list of trusted endpoints. Note that the publicNetworkAccess property is available with apiVersion 2021-01-15 and later. The ipRules property is available with apiVersion 2020-04-01 and later. The ipRangeFilter property is available with apiVersion 2020-03-01 and earlier. You can also restrict access using either Azure Private Link or a service endpoint in an Azure virtual network. See the appropriate Azure documentation for more details about these options. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines an Azure Cosmos DB with limited network access. 
{
    "type": "Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts",
    "apiVersion": "2021-04-15",
    ...
    "properties": {
        ...
        "publicNetworkAccess": "Disabled",
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a network security group that allows access to administrative services.<AltParagraph>The template defines a network security group that allows access to administrative services.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Overly broad configurations expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are subjected to almost continuous scanning and probing by attackers. This is especially problematic when a zero-day exploit for an exposed service is discovered and published (e.g. Heartbleed). Attackers can actively pursue and search for unpatched and exposed systems to exploit. Example 1: The following example template allows unrestricted inbound traffic to a range of ports, including the RDP service port (3389). 
{
    ...
    "name": "sample/securitygroup",
    "type": "Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules",
    "apiVersion": "2020-11-01",
    "properties": {
        "description": "Services Inbound Range",
        "protocol": "Tcp",
        "sourcePortRange": "*",
        "destinationPortRanges": [
            "3333-3389"
        ],
        "sourceAddressPrefix": "*",
        "destinationAddressPrefix": "*",
        "access": "Allow",
        "priority": 100,
        "direction": "Inbound"
    ...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Define Azure Network Security Groups to restrict access to services and make those services only available to as limited an audience as possible. For example, do not make ports that are typically used for management activities of services publicly accessible. Make sure these ports are only available to a restricted pool of systems that require authorized access. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1 by restricting the range of IP addresses that may connect to the RDP service (3389). 
{
    ...
    "name": "sample/securitygroup",
    "type": "Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules",
    "apiVersion": "2020-11-01",
    "properties": {
        "description": "Services Inbound Range",
        "protocol": "Tcp",
        "sourcePortRange": "*",
        "destinationPortRanges": [
            "3333-3389"
        ],
        "sourceAddressPrefix": "10.0.0.1",
        "destinationAddressPrefix": "*",
        "access": "Allow",
        "priority": 100,
        "direction": "Inbound"
    ...
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Azure Blob Storage container that allows anonymous access.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Azure Blob Storage container that allows anonymous access.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Azure Blob Storage containers prevent anonymous access to their Blobs. Insufficient access configurations expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Resources open to public access might unintentionally leak sensitive data. Example 1: The following example template defines an Azure Blob Storage container with the publicAccess property set to Container. This allows anonymous access to all of the Container's blobs and data. 
{
    "type": "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers",
    "apiVersion": "2021-04-01",
    "name": "[format('{0}/default/{1}', parameters('storageAccountName'), parameters('containerName'))]",
    "properties":{
        "publicAccess": "Container"
    }
    ,
    "dependsOn": [
        "[resourceId('Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts', parameters('storageAccountName'))]"
    ]
}
Description.Recommendations:
Restrict access to Azure Blob Storage containers that store confidential data to authorized users. Review your organization's data handling policies when creating resources that are readable by anonymous users. When making a change to access restrictions, identify all dependent systems to limit potential disruptions. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines an Azure Blob Storage container with the publicAccess property set to Private, which allows authorized access only. 
{
    "type": "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers",
    "apiVersion": "2021-04-01",
    "name": "[format('{0}/default/{1}', parameters('storageAccountName'), parameters('containerName'))]",
    "properties":{
        "publicAccess": "Private"
    }
    ,
    "dependsOn": [
        "[resourceId('Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts', parameters('storageAccountName'))]"
    ]
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Azure Container Registry with unrestricted network access.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Azure Container Registry with unrestricted network access.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Recommendations:
Restrict access to services by ensuring that the services are available to as limited an audience as possible. For example, do not make ports that are typically used for service management activities publicly accessible. Make sure these ports are only available to a restricted pool of systems that require authorized access. Limit Azure Container Registry interaction to the scope of IPs that require access to the registry containers. This enables the organization to better protect the assets stored in the registry and reduce its overall surface area of attack. Ensure that the publicNetworkAccess property is set to Disabled. If the registry must be accessed from a public IP range, create the necessary ipRules to specify an allowed list of trusted endpoints. Note that the publicNetworkAccess property is available with apiVersion 2019-12-01-preview and later. You can also restrict access using either Azure Private Link or a service endpoint in an Azure virtual network. See the appropriate Azure documentation for more details about these options. Example 3: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines an Azure Container Registry with restricted network access. 
{
    "name": "[variables('acrName')]",
    "type": "Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries",
    ...
    "properties": {
        "publicNetworkAccess": "Disabled",
        ..
}
Example 4: The following example fixes the problem in Example 2. It defines an Azure Container Registry with a limited list of allowed IP addresses. 
{
    "name": "[variables('acrName')]",
    "type": "Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries",
    ...
    "properties": {
        "publicNetworkAccess": "Enabled",
        "networkRuleSet":
        {
            "defaultAction": "Deny",
            "ipRules":[{
                "action": "Allow",
                "value": "10.0.0.1"
            }]
        }
        ...
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template allows the use of outdated TLS versions.<AltParagraph>The template allows the usage of outdated TLS versions.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
The Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocols provide a protection mechanism to ensure the authenticity, confidentiality, and integrity of data transmitted between a client and web server. Both TLS and SSL have undergone revisions that result in periodic version updates. Each new revision addresses security weaknesses discovered in the previous version. Use of an insecure version of TLS/SSL weakens the strength of the data protection and might allow an attacker to compromise, steal, or modify sensitive information.
Insecure versions of TLS/SSL might exhibit one or more of the following properties:
- No protection against man-in-the-middle attacks - Same key used for authentication and encryption - Weak message authentication control - No protection against TCP connection closing
The presence of these properties might enable an attacker to intercept, modify, or tamper with sensitive data.
Description.Recommendations:
It is highly recommended to force the application to use only the most secure protocols.
Please note that some clients might not support the newer ciphers. It is essential for an organization to upgrade those clients and discontinue the use of outdated and insecure ciphers.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a storage account that does not enforce encryption in transit.<AltParagraph>The template defines a storage account that does not enforce encryption in transit.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Unencrypted communication channels are prone to eavesdropping and tampering. By default, in apiVersion 2019-04-01 and later, Azure storage accounts require a secure connection to respond to requests, but the requirement can be disabled with the supportsHttpsTrafficOnly property. Disabling transfer security exposes the data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering. Example 1: The following example template shows a storage account that does not enforce secure transfer. 
{
    "name": "Storage1",
    "type": "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts",
    "apiVersion": "2021-02-01",
    ...
    "properties": {
        "supportsHttpsTrafficOnly": false
    }
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a security contact without any email notification of security alerts.<AltParagraph>The template defines a security contact without any email notification of security alerts.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Unmonitored systems provide attackers with a way to probe and potentially penetrate defenses without detection. If security personnel are not alerted in a timely fashion to security-related events, they cannot respond to incidents in time to reduce the impact of an attack or breach. Example 1: The following example template successfully defines a security contact but explicitly disables the delivery of security alert email notifications to that contact. 
{
    "name": "Security Officer",
    "type": "Microsoft.Security/securityContacts",
    "apiVersion": "2020-01-01-preview",
    "properties": {
        "emails": "secofficer@example.com",
        "phone": "1212131314",
        "alertNotifications": {
        "state": "Off",
        "minimalSeverity": "High"
        },
        ...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure that critical security alerts are delivered to the relevant personnel. Detecting and responding to incidents quickly reduces the impact to the organization in the event of a breach. With a quick response, the organization can detect targeted hostile and malicious activity and respond appropriately. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1 by setting the alertNotifications/state property to On. 
{
    "name": "Security Officer",
    "type": "Microsoft.Security/securityContacts",
    "apiVersion": "2020-01-01-preview",
    "properties": {
        "emails": "secofficer@example.com",
        "phone": "1212131314",
        "alertNotifications": {
        "state": "On",
        "minimalSeverity": "High"
        },
        ...
}

Description.Abstract: The NamespaceLifecycle admission controller in a Kubernetes API server is disabled.
Description.Explanation:
The deletion of Kubernetes namespace removes all objects in that namespace, including Pods and services. The NamespaceLifecycle admission controller maintains the integrity of Kubernetes systems in two ways. First, it prevents objects from being created in non-existent namespaces or in namespaces undergoing termination. Second, it prevents system reserved namespaces, which contain Kubernetes critical services, from being deleted. The NamespaceLifecycle admission controller is enabled by default but the command to start the Kubernetes API server has disabled it with the --disable-admission-plugin flag. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server. The presence of the NamespaceLifecycle included in the --disable-admission-plugins flag disables the NamespaceLifecycle admission controller. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --disable-admission-plugins=...,NamespaceLifecycle,...
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Do not disable the NamespaceLifecycle admission controller. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the NamespaceLifecycle in the --disable-admission-plugins flag. The NamespaceLifecycle admission controller is enabled by default. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --disable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurityPolicy
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: NamespaceLifecycle Enforcement Disabled

Description.Abstract: Server identity verification of Kubelets is disabled when a Kubernetes API server makes SSL connections.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes API server sends instructions to Kubelets to create workload, queries status of Kubelet-managed resources, and provides optional port-forwarding services to Kubelets. By default, the API server does not verify a Kubelet's serving certificate before establishing connection. This connection is therefore susceptible to a man-in-the-middle attack. Example 1: The following command starts a Kubernetes API server without specifying a root certificate bundle to verify the Kubelet's serving certificate with the --kubelet-certificate-authority flag. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --audit-log-maxage=50
    - --audit-log-maxbackup=20
    - --audit-log-maxsize=200
  image: gcr.io/google_containers/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Provide the API server with a root certificate bundle to verify the Kubelet's serving certificate. Example 2: In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, specify a root certificate bundle to verify the Kubelet's serving certificate with the --kubelet-certificate-authority flag. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --kubelet-certificate-authority=a_path_to_a_cert_file
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing Kubelet Identity Verification

Description.Abstract: The retention period for audit logs is too short.
Description.Explanation:
Log files should be kept long enough to facilitate post-incident analysis and threat detection, as well as to meet compliance requirements. The --audit-log-maxage flag defines the maximum number of days to retain old audit log files. Either the flag is not present in the command to start a Kubernetes API server or the retention period is set to less than 30 days. Example 1: The following command starts a Kubernetes API server and sets --audit-log-maxage flag to 2 (2 days), which is too short. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --audit-log-maxage=2
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Explicitly set the --audit-log-maxage flag to at least 30 days. Do not rely on the default value, which might change. Example 2: In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, set --audit-log-maxage flag to 30 (30 days). 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --audit-log-maxage=30
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Insufficient API server Log Retention

Description.Abstract: The maximum size of audit log files is too small.
Description.Explanation:
The Kubernetes API server automatically rotates log files. To facilitate post-incident analysis and threat detection, as well as to meet compliance requirements, you must retain a sufficient amount of log data. The --audit-log-maxsize flag sets the maximum size in megabytes (MB) of the audit log file before it's automatically rotated. Either this flag is not present in the command to start a Kubernetes API server or the maximum size of the audit log file is set to less than 100 MB. Example 1: The following command starts a Kubernetes API server and sets the --audit-log-maxsize flag to 2 (megabytes), which is insufficient. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - ----audit-log-maxsize=2
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, set the --audit-log-maxsize flag to at least 100. Do not rely on the default value, which might change. Example 2: In the following command to start a Kubernetes API server, the --audit-log-maxsize flag is set to 100 (megabytes). 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --audit-log-maxsize=100
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Insufficient Cloud Log Size

Description.Abstract: An insufficient number of audit logs are retained.
Description.Explanation:
The Kubernetes API server automatically rotates log files. To facilitate post-incident analysis and threat detection, as well as to meet compliance requirements, you must retain a sufficient amount of log data. The --audit-log-maxbackup flag defines the maximum number of log files to retain. Either this flag is not present in the command to start a Kubernetes API server or the maximum number of log files to retain is less than 10. Example 1: The following command starts a Kubernetes API server and sets the --audit-log-maxbackup flag to 2, which insufficiently retains only two log files. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --audit-log-maxbackup=2
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, set the --audit-log-maxbackup flag to at least 10. Do not rely on the default value, which might change. Example 2: In the following command to start a Kubernetes API server, the --audit-log-maxbackup flag is set to 10. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --audit-log-maxbackup=10
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Insufficient Cloud Log Rotation

Description.Abstract: The Kubernetes API server does not authenticate itself to the Kubelet's HTTPS endpoints.
Description.Explanation:
By default, a Kubernetes API server does not authenticate itself to Kubelets when submitting requests. Kubelets, that provide access to a wide variety of resources, cannot verify the authenticity of these requests. Example 1: The following command starts a Kubernetes API server without specifying a client certificate and the corresponding private key with the --kubelet-client-certificate flag and the --kubelet-client-key flag respectively to enable certificate-based authentication to Kubelets. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --audit-log-maxage=50
    - --audit-log-maxbackup=20
    - --audit-log-maxsize=200
    image: gcr.io/google_containers/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Enable certificate-based authentication to the Kubelet's HTTPS endpoint. Example 2: In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, specify a client certificate and the corresponding private key with the --kubelet-client-certificate flag and the --kubelet-client-key flag respectively to enable certificate-based authentication to Kubelets. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
  ...
    - --kubelet-client-certificate=/path/to/apiserver-kubelet-client-certificate.crt
    - --kubelet-client-key=/path/to/apiserver-kubelet-client-key.key
  ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing Kubelet Client Certificate

Description.Abstract: Containerized applications can write to the container's host file system.
Description.Explanation:
By default, a Kubernetes container runtime prevents applications from writing to the root file system of the container. The readOnlyRootFilesystem: false setting disables this restriction, which allows an attacker to tamper with the local file system or write malicious executable to disk. Example 1: The following manifest sets the readOnlyRootFilesystem field to false, which permits applications inside a container to write data to the local disk. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ...
    ...
    securityContext:
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: false
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Prevent containerized applications from writing to the container's root file system. In the Kubernetes Pod manifest, set the readOnlyRootFilesystem field to true. Example 2: The following manifest sets the readOnlyRootFilesystem field to true preventing applications inside a container from writing data to the local disk. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ...
    ...
    securityContext:
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Host Write Access

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes component leaks system information.
Description.Explanation: If profiling is enabled, a component provides performance metrics through a web interface. The performance metrics reveal system data that help an adversary form a plan of attack. Either the --profiling flag is not present in the command to start the component or the flag is set to true.
Description.Recommendations: Disable profiling of the Kubernetes component. Explicitly set the --profiling flag to false. Do not rely on the default value, which might change.

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: API Server Profiling

Description.Abstract: The AlwaysPullImages admission controller is not enabled in a Kubernetes API server.
Description.Explanation:
Pulling a container image from a registry typically requires authorization. Kubernetes nodes, however, cache all images of previously started containers. An attacker can bypass the required authorization by starting a container with a cached image. The AlwaysPullImages admission controller can prevent this bypass. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the AlwaysPullImages admission controller in the --enable-admission-plugins flag. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=PodNodeSelector,LimitRanger
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
The AlwaysPullImages admission controller requires nodes to always pull images from the registry before starting containers so that the registry can verify image ownership for each pull. Example 2: In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, provide a list of admission controllers in the --enable-admission-plugins flag and add the AlwaysPullImages to the list as shown in the following example. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=...,AlwaysPullImages,...
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Image Authorization Bypass

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template explicitly enables public access to an Amazon Redshift cluster.<AltParagraph>The template explicitly enables public access to an Amazon Redshift cluster.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Amazon Redshift clusters are not publicly accessible. Enabling public access to a cluster results in a wider attack surface for the organization. Example 1: The following example template explicitly enables public access to an Amazon Redshift cluster. 
Resources:
  RDCLuster:
    Type: "AWS::Redshift::Cluster"
    Properties:
      PubliclyAccessible: true
      DBName: "rdb"
      MasterUsername: "rduser"
      MasterUserPassword:
        Ref: "MasterUserPassword"
      NodeType: "ds2.xlarge"
      ClusterType: "single-node"
Description.Recommendations:
Restrict communication with the Amazon Redshift cluster to a select pool of systems that have a legitimate need to connect to the cluster. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It explicitly disables public access to the Amazon Redshift cluster by setting the PubliclyAccessible property to false. 
Resources:
  RDCLuster:
    Type: "AWS::Redshift::Cluster"
    Properties:
      PubliclyAccessible: false
      DBName: "rdb"
      MasterUsername: "rduser"
      MasterUserPassword:
        Ref: "MasterUserPassword"
      NodeType: "ds2.xlarge"
      ClusterType: "single-node"

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Improper Redshift Network Access Control

Description.Recommendations:
Restrict communication with the Amazon Redshift cluster to a select pool of systems that have a legitimate need to connect to the cluster. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It explicitly disables public access to the Amazon Redshift cluster by setting the PubliclyAccessible property to false. 
Resources:
  RDCLuster:
    Type: "AWS::Redshift::Cluster"
    Properties:
      PubliclyAccessible: false
      DBName: "rdb"
      MasterUsername: "rduser"

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template explicitly disables transport security for an Amazon DocumentDB cluster.<AltParagraph>The template explicitly disables transport security for an Amazon DocumentDB cluster.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Unencrypted communication channels are prone to eavesdropping and tampering. By default, Amazon DocumentDB clusters enable transport encryption, but it can be disabled with the tls parameter. Disabling transport security exposes the data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering. Example 1: The following example template defines an Amazon DocumentDB cluster with transport encryption disabled. 
Resources:
  DocDBDisabledTLS:
    Type: AWS::DocDB::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Description: docdb cluster parameter group
      Name: test
      Parameters:
        tls: "disabled"
        ttl_monitor: "enabled"
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure that transport encryption is not disabled for Amazon DocumentDB clusters to protect data in transit. Example 2: The following example addresses the issue in Example 1 by defining an Amazon DocumentDB cluster with transport encryption enabled using the tls property. 
Resources:
  DocDBEnabledTLS:
    Type: AWS::DocDB::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Description: docdb cluster parameter group
      Name: test
      Parameters:
        tls: "enabled"
        ttl_monitor: "enabled"

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Insecure DocumentDB Transport

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Amazon Redshift cluster without audit logging.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Amazon Redshift cluster without audit logging.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Amazon Redshift clusters do not capture audit logs. This can allow malicious behavior to go undetected and inhibit forensic analysis in the event of a breach. Example 1: The following example template defines an Amazon Redshift cluster without audit logging. 
Resources:
  RedshiftClusterTest:
    Type: AWS::Redshift::Cluster
    Properties:
      ClusterSubnetGroupName: !Ref RedshiftClusterSubnetGroup
      ClusterType: single-node
      NumberOfNodes: !Ref RedshiftNodeCount
      DBName: !Sub ${DatabaseName}
      IamRoles:
        - !GetAtt RawDataBucketAccessRole.Arn
      MasterUserPassword: !Ref MasterUserPassword
      MasterUsername: !Ref MasterUsername
      PubliclyAccessible: true
      NodeType: dc1.large
      Port: 5439
      VpcSecurityGroupIds:
        - !Sub ${RedshiftSecurityGroup}
Description.Recommendations:
To activate Amazon Redshift audit logging, define a LoggingProperties entity that specifies an Amazon S3 Bucket name where logs are stored. Example 2: The following fixes the template in Example 1 by enabling audit logging. 
Resources:
  RedshiftClusterTest:
    Type: AWS::Redshift::Cluster
    Properties:
      ClusterSubnetGroupName: !Ref RedshiftClusterSubnetGroup
      ClusterType: single-node
      NumberOfNodes: !Ref RedshiftNodeCount
      DBName: !Sub ${DatabaseName}
      IamRoles:
        - !GetAtt RawDataBucketAccessRole.Arn
      MasterUserPassword: !Ref MasterUserPassword
      MasterUsername: !Ref MasterUsername
      PubliclyAccessible: true
      NodeType: dc1.large
      Port: 5439
      VpcSecurityGroupIds:
        - !Sub ${RedshiftSecurityGroup}
      KmsKeyId: K312csd
      LoggingProperties:
        BucketName: "RedshiftDBLogBucket"

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Insufficient Redshift Logging

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Amazon Redshift cluster without audit logging.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Amazon Redshift cluster without audit logging.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Amazon Redshift clusters do not capture audit logs. This can allow malicious behavior to go undetected and inhibit forensic analysis in the event of a breach. Example 1: The following example template defines an Amazon Redshift cluster without audit logging. 
  "Resources": {
    "RedshiftClusterTest": {
      "Properties": {
        "NodeType": "dc1.large",
        "Port": 5439,
        "VpcSecurityGroupIds": [
          "${RedshiftSecurityGroup}"
        ],
        "ClusterSubnetGroupName": "RedshiftClusterSubnetGroup",
        "ClusterType": "single-node"
        "MasterUserPassword": "MasterUserPassword",
        "MasterUsername": "MasterUsername",
        "DBName": "${DatabaseName}",
        "IamRoles": ["RawDataBucketAccessRole.Arn"],
        "PubliclyAccessible": true
      },
      "Type": "AWS::Redshift::Cluster"
    }

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Insufficient Redshift Logging

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Amazon Redshift cluster does not enforce secure communication.<AltParagraph>The Amazon Redshift cluster does not enforce secure communication.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Amazon Redshift clulsters do not require transport encryption. This exposes the data to unauthorized access, tampering, and potential theft. Example 1: The following example template defines am Amazon Redshift cluster that does not enforce transport security. 
Resources:
  RedShiftclusterParms:
    Type: AWS::Redshift::clusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Description: redshift parameter group
      ParameterGroupFamily: redshift-1.0
      Parameters:
        - ParameterName: "require_ssl"
          ParameterValue: "false"
Description.Recommendations:
Enforce transport security for communication with Amazon Redshift clusters using the require_ssl parameter. Example 2: The following fixes the problem in Example 1 by defining an Amazon Redshift cluster that requires SSL communication with clients. 
Resources:
  RedShiftclusterParms:
    Type: AWS::Redshift::clusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Description: redshift parameter group
      ParameterGroupFamily: redshift-1.0
      Parameters:
        - ParameterName: "require_ssl"
          ParameterValue: "true"

Description.Abstract: An etcd instance accepts TLS connections from peers that use self-signed certificates.
Description.Explanation:
Kubernetes keeps sensitive data in an etcd cluster. Therefore, every etcd instance should only accept connections from authenticated and authorized peers and reject any peers that use self-signed certificates for TLS connections. Example 1: The following configuration starts an etcd instance and sets the --peer-auto-tls flag to true. As a result, the etcd instance uses self-signed certificates for TLS connections with peers. 
	...
	spec:
	containers:
	- command:
	...
	- etcd
	...
	- --peer-auto-tls=true
	...
Description.Recommendations:
Forbid the use of automatically generated self-signed certificates for TLS connections between peers. Example 2: The following configuration starts an etcd instance and sets the --peer-auto-tls flag to false. 
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
  ...
      - etcd
  ...
      - --peer-auto-tls=false
  ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Overly Broad Certificate Trust

Description.Abstract: API server identity verification is disabled when Pods make SSL connections.
Description.Explanation:
The Kubernetes controller manager starts without the --root-ca-file flag, which specifies a root Certification Authority (CA) file. As a result, the Kubernetes controller manager does not publish a corresponding root CA certificate to Pods. Without the root CA certificate, the Pods cannot verify the API server's serving certificate before establishing connections. Such connections are susceptible to a man-in-the-middle attack. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager without the --root-ca-file flag. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-controller-manager
    image: k8s.gcr.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.9.7
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
      ...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes controller manager, specify a trusted root CA file. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager and specifies a root CA file with the --root-ca-file flag. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-controller-manager
      - --root-ca-file=a_root_CA.pem
      ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing API Server Identity Verification

Tips.Tip: If the --kubeconfig flag is set and the --root-ca-file flag is not, a controller manager tries to use any root CA file specified in kubeconfig file.

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes API server uses static tokens to authenticate requests.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes API server authenticates requests by comparing bearer tokens to a list kept in a static token file. The token file stores secrets in plaintext and is static in nature. Static token-based authentication is susceptible to brute force attacks and can leak access credentials to attackers in a misconfigured environment. To add, replace, or revoke a token, you must restart the API server. Example 1: Using the --token-auth-file flag, the following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server that authenticates requests by static tokens. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --token-auth-file=<filename>
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Use secure authentication mechanisms such as dynamic tokens and certificates. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the --token-auth-file flag. Instead, the client certificate authentication is enabled by passing the --client-ca-file=SOMEFILE flag. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --client-ca-file=SOMEFILE
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Static Authentication Token

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes API server does not require any authorization for requests.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes API server can authorize a request using one of several authorization modes. The API server does not perform any authorization check in AlwaysAllow mode because it allows all requests. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server with AlwaysAllow as one of the authorization modes. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --authorization-mode=...,AlwaysAllow,...
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Do not use the AlwaysAllow authorization mode. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the AlwaysAllow as one of the authorization modes. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing API Server Authorization

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes container can run in a privileged mode.
Description.Explanation:
By default, a Kubernetes container is denied access to all devices on the host. The privileged field allows the container almost all the same privileges as other processes running on the host. This expands the attack surface and violates the principle of running images with least privileges. Example 1: The Pod runs in a privileged mode by setting privileged: true. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - name: ...
      image: ...
      securityContext:
         privileged: true
...
Description.Recommendations:
Provide the container the needed privileges with the capabilities field. In the container specification, remove the privileged field or apply privileged: false to the securityContext. Example 2: The Pod does not run in a privileged mode by setting privileged: false. The capabilities field defines the least necessary privilege instead. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - name: ...
      image: ...
      securityContext:
        privileged: false
        capabilities:
          add:
          - CAP_NET_ADMIN
...

Reference.Title: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container
Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Privileged Container

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes API server does not use the Node mode to authorize requests made by Kubelets.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes API server can authorize a request using one of several authorization modes. The Node authorization is a special-purpose authorization mode that specifically authorizes API requests made by Kubelets. This ensures that Kubelets have the minimal set of permissions required to operate correctly. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the Node authorization mode. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --authorization-mode=RBAC,Webhook
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, add Node to the list of authorization modes specified in the --authorization-mode flag. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server with Node as one of the authorization modes. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC,Webhook
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing Node Authorization

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes API Server is not configured with any admission controllers.
Description.Explanation:
Admission controllers validate and customize requests to a Kubernetes API Server. They can implement security controls such as rejecting unauthorized privileged requests, enforcing namespace isolation, limiting excessive resource requests, and many more. The API Server does not validate requests because there is no admission controller or the deprecated AlwaysAdmit admission controller is enabled. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server with the AlwaysAdmit admission controller. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=AlwaysAdmit,PodSecurityPolicy
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, provide a list of admission controllers in the --enable-admission-plugins flag and remove the deprecated AlwaysAdmit from the list (if present). Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the AlwaysAdmit admission controller. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --enable-admission-plugins=PodSecurityPolicy
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Improper Admission Controller Access Control

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes API server does not use the role-based access control (RBAC).
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes API server can authorize a request using one of several authorization modes. The role-based access control (RBAC) controls access to computer or network resources based on the roles of individual users within an organization. RBAC is the most secure authorization mode. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the RBAC authorization mode. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --authorization-mode=Node,Webhook
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
In the command to start a Kubernetes API server, add RBAC to the list of authorization modes specified in the --authorization-mode flag. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server with RBAC as one of the authorization modes. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    ...
    - --authorization-mode=RBAC,Node,Webhook
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing RBAC Authorization

Description.Abstract: An etcd instance does not check all incoming HTTPS requests for a client certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority.
Description.Explanation:
Kubernetes keeps sensitive data in an etcd cluster. An etcd instance accepts connections from clients without certificates signed by trusted certificate authorities because the command to start the etcd with the --client-cert-auth flag is set to false. Example 1: The following configuration starts an etcd instance and sets the --client-cert-auth flag to false. 
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
  ...
      - etcd
  ...
      --client-cert-auth=false
  ...
Description.Recommendations:
Make sure that every etcd instance rejects any client that does not use a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority. Example 2: The following configuration starts an etcd instance and sets the --client-cert-auth flag to true so the etcd instance only accepts connections from authenticated clients. 
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
  ...
      - etcd
  ...
      --client-cert-auth=true
  ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Inadequate Certificate Verification

Description.Abstract: Open-access Kubelet APIs leak system information.
Description.Explanation:
To maintain backward compatibility, a Kubelet can serve a subset of its APIs at a read-only port without requiring authentication or authorization. Return values of those APIs contain very detailed specifications and performance metrics of the node that the Kubelet serves as well as metadata of Pods deployed to the node. Example 1: The following configuration sets the Kubelet read-only port to 12345. 
...
kind: KubeletConfiguration
...
readOnlyPort: 12345
...
Description.Recommendations:
Disable the read-only port. Example 2: To disable the read-only port, set readOnlyPort to 0 in a Kubelet configuration file. 
...
kind: KubeletConfiguration
...
readOnlyPort: 0
...

Reference.Title: Set Kubelet parameters via a config file
Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: readOnlyPort Enabled

Tips.Tip: If a Kubelet is started with a Kubelet Configuration file using the --config flag, the default value for readOnlyPort is 0. However, if a Kubelet is started without a configuration file, readOnlyPort is set to the insecure value of 10255.

Description.Abstract: A deprecated flag disables secure communication between a Kubernetes API server and Kubelets.
Description.Explanation:
Connections from a Kubernetes API server to Kubelets often carry sensitive data such as secrets and commands. By default, connections between the API server and the Kubelets are protected in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS). If the --kubelet-https flag is set to false, secure communication is disabled. Example 1: The following configuration disables the secure communication between the API server and the Kubelets because the API server starts with the --kubelet-https flag set to false. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --kublet-https=false
    - --authorization-mode=RBAC
    image: example.domain/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
The --kubelet-https=false flag has been deprecated. Remove it from the command that starts a Kubernetes API server. Example 2: The following configuration starts the Kubernetes API server without the --kubelet-https=false flag. By default, connections between the API server and the Kubelets are protected in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS). 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --authorization-mode=RBAC
    image: example.domain/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Insecure Kubelet Transport

Description.Abstract: A Kubelet does not require any authorization for requests.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubelet authorizes a request using either the AlwaysAllow mode or the Webhook mode. An unspecified authorization mode defaults to AlwaysAllow. The Kubelet does not perform any authorization check in AlwaysAllow mode because it allows all requests. Because Kubelets are the Kubernetes principal agents to manage a worker machine workload, attackers can use uncontrolled requests to gain access to insufficiently protected and security sensitive service APIs. Example 1: The Kubelet does not perform any authorization check because the authorization mode is set to AlwaysAllow. 
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
authorization:
  mode: AlwaysAllow
Description.Recommendations:
Make sure a Kubelet checks the authorization of every request. Example 2: Set authorization to a secure authorization mode such as mode: Webhook in a Kubelet configuration file. 
...
kind: KubeletConfiguration
...
authorization:
  mode: Webhook
...

Reference.Title: Set Kubelet parameters via a config file
Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing Kubelet Authorization

Description.Abstract: The threshold to activate garbage collection of terminated Pods is not specified.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes controller initiates garbage collection to reclaim resources occupied by terminated Pods when their number exceeds a threshold. Although excessive garbage collection degrades performance, the default threshold of 12500 is too high for a typical cluster. Before any garbage collection occurs, the cluster can run low on resources and become unstable. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager without specifying a threshold. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-controller-manager
    image: example.domain/kube-controller-manager:v1.9.7
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
...
Description.Recommendations:
Determine an appropriate threshold for garbage collection based on the size of the cluster. Set the threshold in the command to start a Kubernetes controller manager. Do not rely on the default value, which might change. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager and sets the threshold with the --terminated-pod-gc-threshold=value_of_your_choice flag. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-controller-manager
      - --terminated-pod-gc-threshold=value_of_your_choice
    image: example.domain/kube-controller-manager:v1.9.7
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Missing Garbage Collection Threshold

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes Scheduler accepts external connections.
Description.Explanation:
Kubernetes Scheduler determines where Pods run. By default, a scheduler accepts requests from external connections. From an external connection, an attacker can access insufficiently protected and security sensitive APIs. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes Scheduler without a bind address. 
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-scheduler
    image: example.domain/kube-scheduler:v1.5.2
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
A scheduler is a member of Kubernetes control plane's components that make global decisions about a cluster. Typically, these components all run on the same machine. Reduce the attack surface by limiting Kubernetes Scheduler to serve only local requests. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes Scheduler and sets its bind address to localhost (127.0.0.1). 
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-scheduler
      - --bind-address=127.0.0.1
    image: example.domain/kube-scheduler:v1.5.2
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Unbound Scheduler

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes API server starts without defining a policy to record audit events.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes API server does not log events if there is no audit policy file specified. The event logs contain valuable data used to identify security incidents, monitor policy violations, and assist with non-repudiation controls. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the --audit-policy-file flag. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --audit-log-path=<the log file path>
  image: example.domain/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
  ...
Description.Recommendations:
Specify a valid audit policy file in the command to start a Kubernetes API server. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server and sets an audit policy file using the --audit-policy-file=<the audit policy file path> flag. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --audit-policy-file=<the audit policy file path>
    - --audit-log-path=<the log file path>
  image: example.domain/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Unconfigured API Server Logging

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes API server accepts anonymous requests.
Description.Explanation:
Kubernetes API servers accept anonymous requests by default if the requests are not rejected by other configured authentication methods. Because an API server is the central management entity of a cluster, attackers can use anonymous requests to gain access to insufficiently protected and security sensitive service APIs. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server and permits anonymous requests by setting the --anonymous-auth=true flag. 
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-apiserver
...
      - --anonymous-auth=true
...
Description.Recommendations:
Fortify recommends that a Kubernetes API server authenticates all requests by forbidding anonymous requests. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server and forbids anonymous requests by setting the --anonymous-auth=false flag. 
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-apiserver
...
      - --anonymous-auth=false
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: API Server Anonymous Access

Description.Abstract: Anonymous requests are enabled in a Kubelet configuration.
Description.Explanation:
There is a configuration that permits Kubelets to serve anonymous requests. Anonymous requests are not rejected by any configured authentication method. Because Kubelets are the Kubernetes principal agents to manage a worker machine workload, attackers can use anonymous requests to gain access to insufficiently protected and security sensitive service APIs. Example 1: The following configuration file permits a Kubelet to serve anonymous requests because the anonymous field is set to enabled:true. 
...
kind: KubeletConfiguration
...
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: true
...
Description.Recommendations:
Fortify recommends that Kubelets authenticate all requests by forbidding anonymous requests. Example 2: To forbid anonymous requests, set anonymous to enabled:false in a Kubelet configuration file. 
...
kind: KubeletConfiguration
...
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false
...

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes API server does not save audit events to a log file.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes API server writes audit events to standard output by default. The audit events should be logged to persistent storage. The audit events contain valuable data used to identify security incidents, monitor policy violations, and assist with non-repudiation controls. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the --audit-log-path flag. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --authorization-mode=RBAC
  image: example.domain/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
...
Description.Recommendations:
Define a log file in the command to start a Kubernetes API server. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server and defines a log file with the --audit-log-path=<the log file path> flag. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --audit-log-path=<the log file path>
    - --authorization-mode=RBAC
  image: example.domain/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: API Server Logging Disabled

Description.Abstract: Avoid using a Kubernetes default namespace.
Description.Explanation:
Kubernetes namespaces divide a cluster into manageable chunks. Namespaces provide a scope for names and facilitate the specification of various policies to a subsection of a cluster. By default, Kubernetes allocates a resource to a default namespace. Using a different namespace than the default reduces the impact of mistakes or malicious activities. Example 1: The following configuration sets the namespace of a resource to default. 
...
kind: ...
metadata:
...
namespace: default
spec:
...
Description.Recommendations:
Apart from the special default ServiceAccount and the kubernetes Service namespaces that must remain set to default, always add a definition of a namespace other than default in a manifest and replace any existing definition of namespace: default with a unique name. Example 2: The following configuration sets the namespace of a resource to a name other than default. 
...
kind: ...
metadata:
...
namespace: anything_but_default
spec:
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Default Namespace

Tips.Tip: The namespace of the special default ServiceAccount is default and should not be changed.
The namespace of the special kubernetes Service is default and should not be changed.
Do not use a namespace that starts with kube-, because it is reserved for Kubernetes system namespaces.

Description.Abstract: An etcd instance accepts TLS connections from clients that use self-signed certificates.
Description.Explanation:
Kubernetes keeps sensitive data in an etcd cluster. Therefore, every etcd instance should only accept connections from authenticated and authorized clients and reject any client that uses a self-signed certificate for TLS connections. Example 1: The following configuration starts an etcd instance and sets the --auto-tls flag to true. As a result, the etcd instance uses self-signed certificates for TLS connections with clients. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
...
    - etcd
    ...
    - --auto-tls=true
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
Forbid the use of the automatically generated self-signed certificates for TLS connections with clients. Example 2: The following configuration starts an etcd instance and sets the --auto-tls flag to false. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
...
    - etcd
    ...
    - --auto-tls=false
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: Weak etcd SSL Certificate

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes API server accepts HTTP Basic Authentication.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes API server, the central management entity of a cluster, accepts HTTP Basic Authentication to authenticate users. HTTP Basic Authentication is deprecated and susceptible to brute force attacks and leaks user credentials to attackers in a misconfigured environment. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server and sets the --basic-auth-file=<filename>> flag to use HTTP basic authentication. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-apiserver
      - --basic-auth-file=<filename>
    image: example.domain/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
    livenessProbe:
...
Description.Recommendations:
Do not use HTTP basic authentication. Use secure authentication mechanisms such as dynamic tokens and certificates. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes API server without the --basic-auth-file flag. Instead, the client certificate authentication is enabled by passing the --client-ca-file=SOMEFILE flag. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --client-ca-file=SOMEFILE
    image: example.domain/kube-apiserver-amd64:v1.6.0
    livenessProbe:
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Kubernetes Misconfiguration: HTTP Basic Authentication

Description.Abstract: The CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability is granted to a Pod.
Description.Explanation:
A Kubernetes capability permits a Pod to perform named root actions without giving full root access. The CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability grants the permission to perform the widest possible range of system administration operations to a Pod. Example 1: The following Kubernetes manifest adds the CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability to a container in a Pod. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
...
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        add:
        - CAP_SYS_ADMIN
        - SYS_TIME
        ...
Description.Recommendations:
Remove the CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability from the Pod. Provide the least privileged capability when needed. Example 2: The following Kubernetes manifest does not add the CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability to any container in the Pod. 
...
kind: Pod
...
spec:
  containers:
...
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        add:
        - NET_ADMIN
        - SYS_TIME
        ...

Description.Abstract: A Kubernetes controller manager accepts external connections.
Description.Explanation:
The Kubernetes controller manager monitors the state of a cluster and if required, can make changes in any resources the cluster manages. By default, a controller manager accepts requests from external connections. From an external connection, an attacker can gain access to security sensitive but insufficiently protected APIs. Example 1: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager without a bind address. 
...
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-controller-manager
    - --authentication-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf
    - --authorization-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf
    image: example.domain/kube-controller-manager:v1.9.7
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
A controller manager is a member of Kubernetes control plane's components, which make global decisions about a cluster. These components typically all run on the same machine. Fortify recommends limiting all Kubernetes controller managers to serve only local requests. This reduces the attack surface. Example 2: The following configuration starts a Kubernetes controller manager and sets its bind address to localhost (127.0.0.1). 
...
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
      - kube-controller-manager
      - --bind-address=127.0.0.1
      - --authentication-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf
      - --authorization-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf
    image: example.domain/kube-controller-manager:v1.9.7
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    ...

Description.Abstract: Amazon S3 bucket is created without enabling encryption at rest by default.
Description.Explanation: An Amazon S3 bucket is created without server-side encryption. Encryption mitigates data breaches by making data unreadable to anyone without the proper credentials. As such, encryption at rest is a measure to meet some industrial and government compliance requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI.

Even if there is a default setting that all new objects are encrypted when they are stored in the bucket, authorized clients can still intentionally upload unencrypted data.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a SecurityGroup with insufficient access restrictions. <AltParagraph>The template defines a SecurityGroup with insufficient access restrictions.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Loose access configurations unnecessarily expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are subjected to almost continuous scanning and probing by malicious entities. This is especially problematic when a zero-day exploit for an exposed service is discovered and published (e.g Heartbleed). Attackers can actively pursue and search for unpatched and exposed systems to exploit. 
PSQLSecurityGroup:
  Type: 'AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup'
  Properties:
    VpcId: !Ref VpcId
    GroupDescription: Enable PSQL access via port 5432 to world
    SecurityGroupIngress:
      - CidrIp: 0.0.0.0/0
        FromPort: 5432
        IpProtocol: tcp
        ToPort: 5432
Description.Recommendations:
Define AWS Security Groups to restrict access to services and make those services only available to as limited an audience as possible. For example, do not make ports that are typically used for management activities of services publicly accessible. Make sure these ports are only available to a restricted pool of systems that require authorized access. 
PSQLSecurityGroup:
  Type: 'AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup'
  Properties:
    VpcId: !Ref VpcId
    GroupDescription: Enable PSQL access via port 5432 to admin subnet only
    SecurityGroupIngress:
      - CidrIp: !Ref DbAdminSecGroup
        FromPort: 5432
        IpProtocol: tcp
        ToPort: 5432

Description.Abstract: An Amazon S3 bucket is created without enabling all of the S3 Block Public Access settings.
Description.Explanation: Public access of an S3 bucket due to misconfigurations is a leading cause of data breaches. Although S3 buckets block public access by default, any authorized user can update bucket policies or access control lists (ACLs) to allow public access. Forbid this type of update by enabling the setting of BlockPublicPolicy and BlockPublicAcls respectively under an S3 property of PublicAccessBlockConfiguration. To also guard against any pre-existing overly-permissive bucket policies and ACLs respectively, enable the settings of RestrictPublicBuckets and IgnorePublicAcls.

Reference.Title: There's a Hole in that Bucket!: A Large-scale Analysis of Misconfigured S3 Buckets
Reference.Publisher: ACSAC '18: Proceedings of the 34th Annual Computer Security Applications Conference

Reference.Title: Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage
Fortify Taxonomy | AWS CloudFormation Misconfiguration: Improper S3 Bucket Network Access Control

Tips.Tip: The AWS Account root user who owns an S3 bucket can always update public access policies even if there is a policy to deny updates by any user.

Description.Abstract: Overly broad access specified in an AWS IAM Statement.
Description.Explanation: An AWS IAM Principal defines access to a resource for a user, service, or other entity. In an IAM Statement, there is a definition of an IAM Principal that allows everyone to access an S3 action.
Description.Recommendations:
Remove all instances of the following three types of IAM Principals that allows access of S3 action. 
"Principal":"*"
"Principal":{"AWS":"*"}
"Principal":{"AWS":[...,"*",...]}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an unencrypted SNS topic.<AltParagraph>The template defines an unencrypted SNS topic.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, SNS topics are not encrypted at rest. This potentially exposes the data to unauthorized viewers. Example 1: The following example shows a template that fails to encrypt the SNS topic by neglecting to define an AWS KMS key identifier. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: 2010-09-09
Description: My SNS Topic
Resources:
  MySNSTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Properties:
      Subscription:
        - Endpoint: "MySNSEndpoint"
      Protocol: "sqs"
      TopicName: "SampleTopic"
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure that SNS topics are encrypted at rest to protect any confidential data exchanged over the service. Example 2: The following example template successfully defines an AWS KMS key identifier. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: 2010-09-09
Description: My SNS Topic
Resources:
  MySNSTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Properties:
      Subscription:
        - Endpoint: "MySNSEndpoint"
      Protocol: "sqs"
      TopicName: "MyTopic"
      KmsMasterKeyId: "myKeyID"

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Amazon ElastiCache Replication Group with no encryption. <AltParagraph>The template defines an Amazon ElastiCache Replication Group with no encryption.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Amazon ElastiCache Replication Groups are not encrypted. This exposes the data to unauthorized access and potential theft. Example 1: The following example template defines an Amazon ElastiCache Replication Group with encryption disabled. 
Description: 'ElastiCache redis'
Resources:
  MyReplicationGroup:
    Type: AWS::ElastiCache::ReplicationGroup
    Properties:
      AutomaticFailoverEnabled: true
      CacheNodeType: !Ref CacheNodeType
      CacheParameterGroupName: !Ref CacheParameterGroup
      CacheSubnetGroupName: !Ref CacheSubnetGroupName
      Engine: redis
      EngineVersion: !Ref EngineVersion
      NumNodeGroups: !Ref NumShards
      ReplicasPerNodeGroup: !Ref NumReplicas
      PreferredMaintenanceWindow: 'sat:10:00-sat:08:00'
      SecurityGroupIds:
        - !Ref SecurityGroup
      SnapshotRetentionLimit: !Ref SnapshotRetentionLimit
      SnapshotWindow: '00:00-03:00'
    UpdatePolicy:
      UseOnlineResharding: true
Description.Recommendations:
Enable ElastiCache encryption to protect the data at rest. Amazon ElastiCache Replication Group encryption uses the industry standard AES-256 encryption algorithm to encrypt the data on the server that hosts your database instance. Configure the AtRestEncryptionEnabled property to enable encryption-at-rest for Amazon ElastiCache Replication Groups. Example 2: The following example template defines an Amazon ElastiCache Replication Group with encryption. 
Description: "ElastiCache redis"
Resources:
  MyReplicationGroup:
    Type: AWS::ElastiCache::ReplicationGroup
    Properties:
      AutomaticFailoverEnabled: true
      AtRestEncryptionEnabled: True
      CacheNodeType: !Ref CacheNodeType
      CacheParameterGroupName: !Ref CacheParameterGroup
      CacheSubnetGroupName: !Ref CacheSubnetGroupName
      Engine: redis
      EngineVersion: !Ref EngineVersion
      NumNodeGroups: !Ref NumShards
      ReplicasPerNodeGroup: !Ref NumReplicas
      PreferredMaintenanceWindow: "sat:10:00-sat:08:00"
      SecurityGroupIds:
        - !Ref SecurityGroup
      SnapshotRetentionLimit: !Ref SnapshotRetentionLimit
      SnapshotWindow: "00:00-03:00"
    UpdatePolicy:
      UseOnlineResharding: true

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a CloudWatch Log Group with no retention period.<AltParagraph>The template defines a CloudWatch Log Group with no retention period.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default CloudWatch Log Groups retain logs indefinitely. An unset value indicates that organizational data handling policies have not been consulted in order to set appropriate configurations. This might mean that the organization will incur unnecessary expenses in storing and managing logging events that are no longer relevant. An attacker can launch a Denial of Wallet (DoW) attack by persistently prompting spurious event-logging over an extended period of time, which can impact the organization financially. Example 1: The following example shows a template that fails to define a retention policy. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Resources:
  MyLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
  Properties:
    LogGroupName: Service01LogGroup
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure that CloudWatch Log Groups are configured with an appropriate retention period. It is important to understand organizational data and log management policies in order to reduce any financial overhead and any other related liabilities associated with storing and managing log data. Example 2: The following template defines a retention policy of 100 days. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Resources:
  MyLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
  Properties:
    LogGroupName: Service01LogGroup
    RetentionInDays: 100

Reference.Author: Daniel Kelly, Frank G.Glavin, Enda Barrett

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines publicly accessible AWS API Gateway methods.<AltParagraph>The template defines publicly accessible AWS API Gateway methods.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
AWS API Gateway methods that are publicly accessible can expose the organization to attack. Example 1: The following example template defines publicly accessible AWS API Gateway methods. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Description: "Example"
Resources:
  TestMethod:
    Type: "AWS::ApiGateway::Method"
    Properties:
      RestApiId: !Ref restAPIRes
      ResourceId: !GetAtt
      - restAPIRes
      - RootResourceId
      HttpMethod: GET
      AuthorizationType: NONE
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure that AWS API Gateway methods are only accessible to legitimate or authorized entities. To reduce exposure, do one of the following: - Define an AuthorizationType - Declare that an API key is required with the ApiKeyRequired property Example 2: The following example template defines restricted API Gateway methods. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Description: "Example"
Resources:
  TestMethod:
    Type: "AWS::ApiGateway::Method"
    Properties:
      RestApiId: !Ref restAPIRes
      ResourceId: !GetAtt
      - restAPIRes
      - RootResourceId
      HttpMethod: GET
      AuthorizationType: AWS_IAM

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a Neptune DB cluster without encryption of data at rest.<AltParagraph>The template defines a Neptune DB cluster without encryption of data at rest.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Neptune DB clusters are not encrypted. This exposes the data to potential theft and unauthorized access by attackers. Example 1: The following example template fails to enable encryption at rest. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: 2010-09-09
Description: My Neptune DB cluster
Resources:
  NeptuneDBCluster:
    Type: "AWS::Neptune::DBCluster"
    Properties:
      BackupRetentionPeriod: 10
      DBClusterIdentifier: MyDBClusterIdentifier
      DBClusterParameterGroupName: MyNeptuneDBClusterParameterGroup
      DBSubnetGroupName: MyNeptuneDBSubnetGroup
      IamAuthEnabled: true
      Port: 8080
      PreferredBackupWindow: NeptuneDBClusterPreferredBackupWindow
      PreferredMaintenanceWindow: NeptuneDBClusterPreferredMaintenanceWindow
Description.Recommendations:
Fortify recommends that you enable Neptune DB cluster encryption to protect the data at rest. Example 2: The following example template successfully defines a Neptune DB cluster with encryption enabled for data at rest. 
Description: My Neptune DB cluster
Resources:
  NeptuneDBCluster:
    Type: "AWS::Neptune::DBCluster"
    Properties:
      BackupRetentionPeriod: 10
      DBClusterIdentifier: MyDBClusterIdentifier
      DBClusterParameterGroupName: MyNeptuneDBClusterParameterGroup
      DBSubnetGroupName: MyNeptuneDBSubnetGroup
      IamAuthEnabled: true
      Port: 8080
      PreferredBackupWindow: NeptuneDBClusterPreferredBackupWindow
      PreferredMaintenanceWindow: NeptuneDBClusterPreferredMaintenanceWindow
      StorageEncrypted: true
