Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an ElastiCache replication group without transport encryption.<AltParagraph>The template defines an ElastiCache replication group without transport encryption.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Unencrypted communication channels are prone to eavesdropping and tampering. By default, ElastiCache replication group transport encryption is disabled. This exposes the data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering. Example 1: The following example template defines an ElastiCache replication group without transport encryption enabled. 
Resources:
  ReplicationGroup:
    DeletionPolicy: Snapshot
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot
    Type: AWS::ElastiCache::ReplicationGroup
    Properties:
      ReplicationGroupDescription: !Ref 'AWS::StackName'
      AtRestEncryptionEnabled: true
      CacheNodeType: !Ref CacheNodeType
      CacheParameterGroupName: !Ref CacheParameterGroup
      CacheSubnetGroupName: !Ref CacheSubnetGroupName
      Engine: redis
      EngineVersion: !Ref EngineVersion
      NumNodeGroups: !Ref NumShards
      ReplicasPerNodeGroup: !Ref NumReplicas
      PreferredMaintenanceWindow: 'sat:07:00-sat:08:00'
      SecurityGroupIds:
      - !Ref SecurityGroup
      SnapshotRetentionLimit: !Ref SnapshotRetentionLimit
      SnapshotWindow: '00:00-03:00'
    UpdatePolicy:
      UseOnlineResharding: true
Description.Recommendations:
Fortify recommends that you enable ElastiCache encryption to protect the data in transit. Example 2: The following example addresses the issue in Example 1 by defining an ElastiCache replication group with transport encryption enabled using the TransitEncryptionEnabled property. 
Resources:
  ReplicationGroup:
    DeletionPolicy: Snapshot
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot
    Type: AWS::ElastiCache::ReplicationGroup
    Properties:
      ReplicationGroupDescription: !Ref 'AWS::StackName'
      AtRestEncryptionEnabled: true
      CacheNodeType: !Ref CacheNodeType
      CacheParameterGroupName: !Ref CacheParameterGroup
      CacheSubnetGroupName: !Ref CacheSubnetGroupName
      Engine: redis
      EngineVersion: !Ref EngineVersion
      NumNodeGroups: !Ref NumShards
      ReplicasPerNodeGroup: !Ref NumReplicas
      PreferredMaintenanceWindow: 'sat:07:00-sat:08:00'
      SecurityGroupIds:
      - !Ref SecurityGroup
      SnapshotRetentionLimit: !Ref SnapshotRetentionLimit
      SnapshotWindow: '00:00-03:00'
      TransitEncryptionEnabled: true
    UpdatePolicy:
      UseOnlineResharding: true

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an access key for your AWS account root user.<AltParagraph>The template defines an access key for your AWS account root user.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Defining access keys for your AWS root user account places all your AWS resources at risk if the key is ever compromised. Example 1:The following example template creates an access key for the root user account. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Resources:
  SecKeys:
    Type: AWS::IAM::AccessKey
    Properties:
      UserName: Root
Description.Recommendations:
Following the principle of least privilege, create a dedicated IAM user with the least rights required to perform the necessary activities. Example 2: The following example template creates an access key for a limited privilege user that is expected to perform a limited set of operations on the organization's AWS infrastructure. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Resources:
  SecKeys:
    Type: AWS::IAM::AccessKey
    Properties:
      UserName: RDSAdmin

Description.Abstract: An Amazon S3 bucket is created without enabling access logging
Description.Explanation: Amazon S3 buckets do not save access logs by default. The logs, however, contain value data used to identify security incidents, monitor policy violations, and assist with non-repudiation controls.
Description.Recommendations:
To enable Amazon S3 server access logging, add a LoggingConfiguration property, which defines where logs are stored and assigns a prefix for all log object keys as follows: 
...
Resources:
  S3Bucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      LoggingConfiguration:
      DestinationBucketName: someLoggingBucket
      LogFilePrefix: someLogPrefix
...

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a trail without log file validation. <AltParagraph>The template defines a trail without log file validation.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, CloudTrail log file validation is disabled, which prevents investigators from asserting that there has been no external tampering with CloudTrail log files. A direct result of this is that an attacker with the necessary privileges can perform harmful configuration changes and cover their tracks by modifying CloudTrail logs. Example 1: The following is an example of a trail with log file validation disabled by setting EnableLogFileValidation to false. Omitting the property results in having the default value set to false as well. 
myTrail:
  DependsOn:
    - BucketPolicy
  Type: AWS::CloudTrail::Trail
  Properties:
    S3BucketName:
      Ref: S3Bucket
      IsLogging: true
      EnableLogFileValidation: false
Description.Recommendations:
Fortify recommends that you enable CloudTrail log file validation to collect digest files, which can be used to confirm whether anyone has tampered with the log files. Example 2: The following example enables validation by setting the EnableLogFileValidation to true. 
myTrail:
  DependsOn:
    - BucketPolicy
  Type: AWS::CloudTrail::Trail
  Properties:
    S3BucketName:
    Ref: S3Bucket
    IsLogging: true
    EnableLogFileValidation: true

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines a wildcard lambda principal.<AltParagraph>The template defines a wildcard lambda principal.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
A wildcard configuration for lambda principals violates the least privilege principle and allows an attacker to invoke the lambda from any account. Example 1: The following example template defines a wildcard lambda principal. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Description: Lambda Permission
Resources:
  LambdaPerm:
  Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
  Properties:
    FunctionName: !GetAtt function.Arn
    Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
    Principal: "*"
    SourceAccount: !Ref "AWS::AccountId"
    SourceArn: !GetAtt bucket.Arn
Description.Recommendations:
Explicitly define lambda principals to restrict invocation of the lambda function to authorized accounts and services. Example 2: The following example template defines a specific principal authorized to invoke the lambda. 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Description: Lambda Permission
Resources:
  LambdaPerm:
  Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
  Properties:
    FunctionName: !GetAtt function.Arn
    Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
    Principal: s3.amazonaws.com
    SourceAccount: !Ref "AWS::AccountId"
    SourceArn: !GetAtt bucket.Arn

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the template defines an Amazon DocumentDB instance with no encryption.<AltParagraph>The template defines an Amazon DocumentDB instance with no encryption.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>

Example 2: The following example shows a template that defines an Amazon DocumentDB with encryption. 
Resources:
  DocDBDInst:
    Type: AWS::DocDB::DBCluster
    Properties:
      MasterUsername: myUser
      MasterUserPassword: password
      StorageEncrypted: true

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration disables the monitoring service of a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster.<AltParagraph>A Terraform script disables the monitoring service of a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster sends metrics from Pods to the Stackdriver Kubernetes Engine Monitoring Service. The Terraform script sets up a GKE cluster and explicitly disables the monitoring service. The absence of metrics undermines proper detection of and prompt response to security events. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that disables the monitoring service of a GKE cluster by setting monitoring_service to none. 
resource "google_container_cluster" "cluster-demo" {
    name               = "name-demo"
    location           = "us-central1-a"
    monitoring_service = "none"
    ...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Remove the monitoring_service setting so the cluster sends metrics to the default monitoring service. Alternatively, set monitoring_service to any of the supported services. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It sets the monitoring service of the GKE cluser to the Stackdriver Kubernetes Engine Logging Service. 
resource "google_container_cluster" "cluster-demo" {
    name               = "name-demo"
    location           = "us-central1-a"
    monitoring_service = "monitoring.googleapis.com/kubernetes"
    ...
}

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | GCP Terraform Misconfiguration: Insufficient GKE Cluster Monitoring

Description.Explanation: Granting allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers a Cloud KMS CryptoKey role gives anyone access to sensitive data.
Description.Recommendations: Avoid granting any Cloud KMS CryptoKey roles to allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers. Assign specific users or groups to a Cloud KMS CryptoKey role on an as-needed basis.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Compute Engine instance does not use a customer-supplied encryption key to protect the disk encryption key.<AltParagraph>A Compute Engine instance does not use a customer-supplied encryption key to protect the disk encryption key.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Google Cloud Compute Engine encrypts all data at rest. A customer-supplied encryption key (CSEK), if specified, encrypts the data encryption keys. Google does not store any CSEK on a Compute Engine instance and cannot access the protected data unless the correct CSEK is provided. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform Configuration that defines a persistent disk for a Compute Engine instance. The disk_encryption_key block is missing so there is no CSEK to protect the data encryption keys. 
resource "google_compute_disk" "compute-disk-demo" {
    name  = "test-disk"
    type  = "pd-ssd"
}
Description.Recommendations:
Specify a customer-supplied encryption key (CSEK) for any persistent disk that keeps sensitive data. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. The disk_encryption_key block specifies a CSEK stored in the Google Cloud KMS (kms_key_self_link) to protect the data encryption keys. 
resource "google_compute_disk" "compute-disk-demo" {
    name  = "test-disk"
    type  = "pd-ssd"
    disk_encryption_key {
        kms_key_self_link = "foo-bar-key"
        sha256 = ...
    }
}
Using customer-managed keys requires organizations to fully manage key lifecycle activities including issuance, storage, revocation, and rotation. Organizations should review their compliance requirements and determine whether to use customer-managed keys.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Ansible task defines an Azure SQL Database instance with unrestricted network access.<AltParagraph>The Ansible task defines an Azure SQL Database instance with unrestricted network access.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Azure SQL Database instances with unrestricted ranges of allowable IP addresses unnecessarily broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are subjected to almost continuous scanning and probing by attackers. Example 1: The following example Ansible task defines an overly exposed Azure SQL Database instance. 
- name: Create Firewall Rule
  azure.azcollection.azure_rm_sqlfirewallrule:
    resource_group: orgTestGroup
    server_name: orgSQLServer
    name: SQLServerFWRule
    start_ip_address: 0.0.0.0
    end_ip_address: 255.255.255.255
Description.Recommendations:
Configure Azure SQL Database firewall rules to accept connections from a restricted range of IP addresses. To specify trusted sources, create an Azure Ansible SQL firewall rule with appropriate start_ip_address and end_ip_address values. Example 2: The following example Ansible task reduces the risk in Example 1. It restricts Azure SQL Database instance access to a restricted range of IP addresses. 
- name: Create Firewall Rule
  azure.azcollection.azure_rm_sqlfirewallrule:
    resource_group: orgTestGroup
    server_name: orgSQLServer
    name: SQLServerFWRule
    start_ip_address: 196.12.111.0
    end_ip_address: 196.12.111.20

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Ansible task defines an Amazon RDS instance with public access.<AltParagraph>An Ansible task defines an Amazon RDS instance with public access.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
A publicly accessible Amazon RDS instance unnecessarily broadens an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are subjected to almost continuous scanning and probing by attackers. Example 1: The following Ansible task sets up an RDS instance with public access because publicly_accessible is set to true. 
- name: createdb
  community.aws.rds_instance:
    db_instance_identifier: test-db
    engine: aurora
    instance_type: db.t2.small
    username: "{{ username }}"
    password: "{{ password }}"
    cluster_id: test-cluster
    publicly_accessible: true
Description.Recommendations:
Explicitly disable the public access of an RDS instance. Do not rely on the default parameter value, which might change. Example 2: The following Ansible task creates an RDS instance with public access disabled by setting publicly_accessible to false. 
- name: createdb
  community.aws.rds_instance:
    db_instance_identifier: test-db
    engine: aurora
    storage_encrypted: yes
    instance_type: db.t2.small
    username: "{{ username }}"
    password: "{{ password }}"
    cluster_id: test-cluster
    publicly_accessible: false

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Ansible task defines an Amazon CloudFront Distribution that does not secure data in transit.<AltParagraph>An Ansible task defines an Amazon CloudFront Distribution that does not secure data in transit.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Amazon CloudFront Distribution can be misconfigured to allow unauthenticated or unencrypted communication, or use an outdated protocol. Such misconfigurations can cause compromise and allow an attacker, residing on a shared network, to snoop and tamper with data in transit.
Description.Recommendations: It is important to protect data in transit from unauthorized disclosure and modification. Use secure protocols such as HTTPS and TLS to exchange data with the server whenever possible.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration does not set the cluster network mode to VPC-native.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration does not set the cluster network mode to VPC-native.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
GKE supports two cluster network modes: routes-based and VPC-native. VPC-native clusters use alias IP address ranges to route traffic from one Pod in a node to another Pod. This allows precise IP-based policies and firewall rules for Pods. In contrast, an entire node is the finest granularity level of control in routes-based clusters. Example 1: The following example Terraform configuration does not enable a VPC-native cluster by setting networking_mode to ROUTES. 
resource "google_container_cluster" "cluster_demo" {
...
  networking_mode = "ROUTES"
..
}
Description.Recommendations:
Set the cluster network mode to VPC-native. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It enables a VPC-native cluster by setting networking_mode to VPC_NATIVE. 
resource "google_container_cluster" "cluster_demo" {
...
  networking_mode = "VPC_NATIVE"
...
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration does not define any authorized networks to restrict GKE control planes access.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration does not define any authorized networks to restrict GKE control planes access.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
The GKE control plane makes global decisions about a cluster and by default, many of its API endpoints are publicly accessible. Adding authorized networks using an allow list can provide network level protection for control plane access. Example 1: The following example Terraform configuration sets up a public cluster without defining any authorized networks in the master_authorized_networks_config block. As a result, the GKE control plane API endpoints are publicly accessible. 
resource "google_container_cluster" "cluster_demo" {
  name = "name-demo"
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration enables legacy ABAC authorization on a GKE cluster.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration enables legacy ABAC authorization on a GKE cluster.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) is disabled on new clusters that run GKE version 1.8 and later. ABAC can statically grant a specific user or a group access to a resource in addition to those provided by Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) or Identity and Access Management (IAM). This complicates authorization administration and undermines the centralized access control. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that enables legacy ABAC authorization on a GKE cluster by setting enable_legacy_abac to true. 
resource "google_container_cluster" "container_cluster_demo" {
...
  enable_legacy_abac = true
...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Never enable legacy ABAC authorization, and instead use RBAC, IAM, or both to control access to the GKE cluster. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It disables legacy ABAC authorization on a GKE cluster by setting enable_legacy_abac to false. 
resource "google_container_cluster" "container_cluster_demo" {
...
  enable_legacy_abac = false
...
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration permits SSL policies with weak cipher suites for proxy load balancers.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration permits SSL policies with weak cipher suites for proxy load balancers.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
The Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocols provide a protection mechanism to ensure the authenticity, confidentiality, and integrity of data transmitted between a client and web server. Both TLS and SSL have undergone revisions that result in periodic version updates. Each new revision addresses security weaknesses discovered in the previous version. Use of an insecure version of TLS/SSL weakens the data protection and might allow an attacker to compromise, steal, or modify sensitive information. Insecure versions of TLS/SSL might exhibit one or more of the following properties: - No protection against man-in-the-middle attacks - Same key used for authentication and encryption - Weak message authentication control - No protection against TCP connection closing The presence of these properties might enable an attacker to intercept, modify, or tamper with sensitive data. Example 1: The following example Terraform configuration defines an SSL policy that permits the proxy load balancer to allow the use of weak SSL cipher suites by setting profile to COMPATIBLE. 
resource "google_compute_ssl_policy" "policy-demo" {
...
  profile = "COMPATIBLE"
...
}
Example 2: The following example Terraform configuration that defines a custom SSL policy that specifically permits the proxy load balancer to allow the use of a weak SSL cipher suite named TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. 
resource "google_compute_ssl_policy" "policy-demo" {
...
  profile = "CUSTOM"
  min_tls_version = "TLS_1_2"
  custom_features = ["TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256", "TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256", "TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA"]
...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Use the pre-configured RESTRICTED profile for the load balancer SSL policy. This Google-managed profile ensures that the SSL policy is up-to-date and incorporates best practices. Example 3: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1 and Example 2 by setting profile to RESTRICTED. 
resource "google_compute_ssl_policy" "policy-demo" {
...
profile = "RESTRICTED"
...
}

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | GCP Terraform Misconfiguration: Insecure Load Balancer Transport

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration allows the auto-creation of a project-wide network with weak access control.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration allows the auto-creation of a project-wide network with weak access control.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, a new Google Cloud project starts with a project-wide network. The default network is pre-populated with firewall rules that permit unrestricted communication among Compute Engine instances in the same project and expose security sensitive ports of all instances to the public. The affected ports include TCP 22 (SSH) and TCP 3389 (RDP). Any insufficiently protected instance is susceptible to unauthorized access. Example 1: The following example Terraform configuration enables the auto-creation of a project-wide network by setting auto_create_network to true. 
resource "google_project" "project-demo" {
...
  auto_create_network = true
...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Never allow the creation of the default network when setting up a Google Cloud project. Create Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks and configure firewall rules based on organization and security requirements. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It disables the auto-creation of a default project-wide network by setting auto_create_network to false. 
resource "google_project" "project-demo" {
...
  auto_create_network = false
...
}
Example 3: The following Terraform configuration example provides another way to fix the problem in Example 1. Terraform documentation recommends the use of the compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation organizational policy constraint to remove the default network instead of setting auto_create_network to false as shown in Example 2. 
resource "google_organization_policy" "policy-demo" {
...
  constraint = "compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation"
...
  boolean_policy {
    enforced = true
  }
...
}

Reference.Title: Pre-populated rules in the default network
Reference.Author: Google Cloud

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | GCP Terraform Misconfiguration: Google Project Network Access Control

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the configuration defines an Azure Service that does not enforce encrypted communication.<AltParagraph>The configuration defines an Azure Service that does not enforce encrypted communication.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Unencrypted communication channels are prone to eavesdropping and tampering. Servicing client requests over an insecure communications channel allows attackers to perform man-in-the-middle attacks, and gives them access to read or modify the data in transit.
Description.Recommendations: Consider enabling transport encryption to ensure that all data exchange is performed over encrypted channels and inhibit man-in-the-middle attacks. Please note that such a change can disrupt your current communications and that careful planning should be employed to remediate this issue.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration sets up a Compute Engine instance that enables IP forwarding.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration sets up a Compute Engine instance that enables IP forwarding.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Failure to block unwanted network traffic expands a cloud service's attack surface. By default, IP forwarding is disabled in a Compute Engine instance. IP forwarding allows sending and receiving packets with non-matching source or destination IPs. An attacker can exploit this by routing packets through the Compute Engine instance to bypass network access control. Example 1: The following Terraform configuration enables IP forwarding by setting can_ip_forward to true. 
resource "google_compute_instance" "compute_instance_demo" {
  ...
  can_ip_forward = true
  ...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Disable IP forwarding unless the Computer Engine instance intentionally serves as a network router. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It disables IP forwarding by setting can_ip_forward to false. 
resource "google_compute_instance" "compute_instance_demo" {
  ...
  can_ip_forward = false
  ...
}

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | GCP Terraform Misconfiguration: Compute Engine IP Forwarding Enabled

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration sets up a Compute Engine instance without enabling all recommended Shield VM options.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration sets up a Compute Engine instance without enabling all recommended Shield VM options.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Every cloud service security feature has a unique ability to prevent or mitigate a known threat. Any feature disabled by intent or mistake offers no protection. Disabling any Shield VM option allows an attacker to bypass implemented security restrictions for a guest operating system on a Compute Engine instance. Recommended Shield VM options (and their corresponding Terraform configuration identifiers) are as follows: - Integrity Monitoring (enable_integrity_monitoring) - Secure Boot (enable_secure_boot) - Virtual Trusted Platform Module (enable_vtpm) Example 1: The following Terraform configuration sets enable_integrity_monitoring to false in the shielded_instance_config block. Not all recommended Shield VM options are enabled. 
resource "google_compute_instance" "compute_instance_demo" {
  ...
  shielded_instance_config {
    enable_integrity_monitoring = false
    enable_secure_boot = true
    enable_vtpm = true
  }
  ...
}

Reference.Title: Modifying Shielded VM options on a VM instance
Reference.Author: Google Cloud

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | GCP Terraform Misconfiguration: Compute Engine Shielded VM Option Disabled

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration sets up a Google Storage Bucket that allows the use of Access Control Lists for controlling permissions.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration sets up a Google Storage Bucket that allows the use of Access Control Lists for controlling permissions.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Mismanagement of permissions increases the risk of unauthorized access to or modification of restricted data. To define user permission for access to buckets and objects in buckets, Google Cloud Storage offers two systems: Access Control Lists (ACLs) and Identity and Access Management (IAM). IAM can be used throughout Google Cloud, while only Cloud Storage supports ACLs. Enabling Uniform Bucket-level Access prevents ACLs from granting permission. This ensures IAM is the only system to manage all access control of Google Cloud resources. Example 1: The following Terraform configuration permits using ACLs alongside IAM to grant access to the storage bucket by setting uniform_bucket_level_access to false. 
resource "google_storage_bucket" "bucket-demo" {
...
  uniform_bucket_level_access = false
...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Do not use ACLs to administrate bucket permissions. Use only IAM to grant user access to buckets and objects. Example 2: The following Terraform configuration fixes the problem in Example 1. It disallows access granted by bucket ACLs by setting uniform_bucket_level_access to true. 
resource "google_storage_bucket" "bucket-demo" {
...
  uniform_bucket_level_access = true
...
}
Example 3: The following Terraform configuration shows another way to resolve the issue in Example 1. The storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess organizational policy constraint enforces Uniform Bucket-level Access for an entire organization. 
resource "google_organization_policy" "policy-demo" {
...
  constraint = "storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess"
...
  boolean_policy {
    enforced = true
  }
...
}

Reference.Title: Organization policy constraints for Cloud Storage
Reference.Author: Google Cloud

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | GCP Terraform Misconfiguration: Cloud Storage Bucket Uniform Access Disabled

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration assigns a service account role to an IAM user.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration assigns a service account role to an IAM user.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Mismanagement of permissions increases the risk of unauthorized access to or modification of data and undermines service availability.
A service account is a special Google account used by an application or a VM instead of a person, which uses sensitive permissions to run automated processes or make API requests on behalf of end users. It should be carefully managed, controlled, and audited, so it can be trusted. Assigning a service account role to an IAM user, which typically represents a person, weakens the security control.
Description.Recommendations: Do not assign any service account roles, which include roles/iam.serviceAccountUser and roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator, to an IAM user.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration defines a VPC Firewall rule that allows incoming connections to a security-sensitive port.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration defines a VPC Firewall rule that allows incoming connections to a security-sensitive port.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Failure to block unwanted network traffic expands a cloud service's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are subjected to almost continuous scanning and probing by malicious entities.
Description.Recommendations: Define firewall rules that restrict network access to security-sensitive services. Ensure the services are available to as limited an audience as possible.

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | GCP Terraform Misconfiguration: Overly Permissive VPC Firewall

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration uses a module from an untrusted source.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration uses a module from an untrusted source.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Software modules from untrusted software supply chains might not be secure. Attackers can exploit the weakness of any poorly managed supply chain to insert malicious code. A Terraform module is a pre-built set of configuration files. Modules make it easier and faster to get cloud services up and running. Many sources provide modules, including but not limited to the Terraform Registry, local directories, source repositories, and cloud storage. However, only a fraction of modules published in the Terraform Registry are systematically and continuously verified among all sources. A verified module listed in the Terraform Registry is a module that is in active maintenance and tested for compatibility but is not necessarily secure by design.
Description.Recommendations: Only use modules whose security is assured on an ongoing basis by a trusted organization.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration sets up an App Engine without enforcing SSL for all connections.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration sets up an App Engine without enforcing SSL for all connections.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: By default, an App Engine application accepts unencrypted and unsecured connections. These connections expose data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering.
Description.Recommendations: Enforce SSL for all connections. Do not rely on the default settings, which might change.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration sets up a domain for an App Engine application without HTTPS support.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration sets up a domain for an App Engine application without HTTPS support.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, the domain for an App Engine application accepts unencrypted and unsecured connections. These connections expose data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that does not contain an ssl_settings block for the domain named example.com. As a result, the custom domain for the App Engine application does not support HTTPS. 
resource "google_app_engine_domain_mapping" "domain_mapping" {
  domain_name = "example.com"
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration allows insecure HTTP requests to trigger a Cloud Function.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration permits insecure HTTP requests to trigger a Cloud Function.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, an HTTP trigger enables a Cloud Function to run in response to HTTPS requests only. Allowing insecure HTTP requests exposes data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an HTTP trigger that fails to enforce HTTPS endpoints by setting https_trigger_security_level to SECURE_OPTIONAL. 
resource "google_cloudfunctions_function" "demo_function" {
...
  trigger_http = true
  https_trigger_security_level = "SECURE_OPTIONAL"
...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Make all function endpoints require HTTPS. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. The function endpoint requires HTTPS by setting https_trigger_security_level to SECURE_ALWAYS. 
resource "google_cloudfunctions_function" "demo_function" {
...
  trigger_http = true
  https_trigger_security_level = "SECURE_ALWAYS"
...
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a Terraform configuration allows clients to connect to an Edge Cache service using HTTP or HTTPS.<AltParagraph>A Terraform configuration allows clients to connect to an Edge Cache service using HTTP or HTTPS.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
By default, an Edge Cache service accepts unencrypted and unsecured connections. These connections expose data to unauthorized access, potential theft, and tampering. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an Edge Cache service that does not require clients to use TLS for communication by setting require_tls to false. 
resource "google_network_services_edge_cache_service" "srv_demo" {
...
  require_tls = false
...
}
Description.Recommendations:
Ensure Edge Cache serves sensitive data only through TLS-encrypted connections. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. The Edge Cache service requires clients to use TLS for communication by setting require_tls to true. 
resource "google_network_services_edge_cache_service" "srv_demo" {
...
  require_tls = true
...
}

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the automount of API credentials is not disabled.<AltParagraph>The automount of API credentials is not disabled.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Unless otherwise specified, any newly created Pod is automatically assigned a default service account. For each service account, an API access token is automatically generated and made available in a mounted directory. Attackers can use the access token in any compromised Container to gain access to insufficiently protected and security-sensitive service APIs. The automounting of API credentials for the default service account of a Pod is not disabled because automountServiceAccountToken is not defined or the configuration of the default service account contains the automountServiceAccountToken: true setting. Example 1: API credentials for the default service account of a Pod are automounted if the automountServiceAccountToken is not defined or is set to true, as in this example. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: demo-namespace
automountServiceAccountToken: true
...
Example 2: API credentials are automounted for a Pod because there is an automountServiceAccountToken: true setting in the default service account as in this example. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
  ...
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: true
  ...
Description.Recommendations:
Unless it is essential to provide the Pod with the ability to interact with the Kubernetes API server, opt out of automounting API credentials in a ServiceAccount or Pod configuration file. In general, setting the automountServiceAccountToken field to false in a Pod configuration opts the Pod out of automounting API credentials. However, Pods can also be set up by other workload resources, including but not limited to CronJob, DaemonSet, Deployment, Job, ReplicaSet, ReplicationController, and StatefulSet. Check the relevant version of the resource schema to ascertain the correct location to set the needed field. Example 3: In the following ServiceAccount configuration, the default service account is opted out of automounting API credentials by specifying automountServiceAccountToken: false. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: demo-namespace
automountServiceAccountToken: false
...
Example 4: In the following Pod configuration, the Pod is opted out of automounting API credentials by specifying automountServiceAccountToken: false. 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
  ...
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  ...

Description.Explanation: Hardcoding a password allows all project developers to view the password. It also makes fixing the problem difficult. After the code is in production, no one can change the password without patching the software. If the account protected by the password is compromised, the system's owners must choose between security and availability.
Description.Recommendations: Use the Mule runtime engine to retrieve sensitive configuration properties from a secure source such as a Secure Configuration Properties file and a credentials vault.

Description.Explanation: The Mule Database Connector should force encrypted transport and verify database server certificates. Description.Recommendations: Configure database connection properties to force encrypted transport and verify server certificates.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, the Mule configuration specifies a TLS connection without the server certificate validation check.<AltParagraph>The Mule configuration specifies a TLS connection without the server certificate validation check.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Certification verification is essential to confirm the counterpart's identity for secure communication. A tls:context element defines a set of TLS connection configurations. Among the configurations, the tls:trust-store element specifies a file that contains certificates from trusted Certificate Authorities that a client uses to verify a certificate presented by a server. By default, the Mule runtime engine verifies the server certificate for every TLS connection. However, if the value of the insecure attribute of the tls:trust-store element is true, server certificates are accepted without verification. Example 1: The following Mule configuration sets the insecure attribute to true. As a result, the Mule runtime engine does not verify the server certificate of any connection with the TLS context named demoTlsContext. Such a connection is susceptible to a man-in-the-middle attack. 
...
<tls:context name="demoTlsContext">
...
    <tls:trust-store ... insecure="true" ... />
...
<tls:context/>
...
Description.Recommendations:
In production environments, always verify TLS server certificates. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It forces certificate verification by setting the insecure attribute of the tls:trust-store element to false. 
...
<tls:context name="demoTlsContext">
...
    <tls:trust-store ... insecure="false" ... />
...
<tls:context/>
...

Reference.Title: Configure TLS with Keystores and Truststores
Reference.Author: MuleSoft LLC, a Salesforce company

Description.Abstract: In on line , the OpenAPI specification is missing a global security definition.The OpenAPI specification is missing a global security definition.
Description.Explanation:
Global security requirements inform API consumers of the authentication and authorization parameters required to successfully interact with the API. An absent global security definition might enable attackers to interact with sensitive API endpoints and allow them to perform operations that should be restricted to specific user accounts with specific privileges. Example 1: The following OpenAPI specification neglects to declare a global security definition. APIs that implement this specification might be vulnerable to unauthorized or unauthenticated access to sensitive operations. 
    openapi: 3.0.3
    info:
      title: My API
      version: 1.0.0
    ...
Description.Recommendations:
The global security definition provides the default authentication and authorization requirements for API operations. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines a global security definition. 
    openapi: 3.0.3
    info:
      title: My API
      version: 1.0.0
    security:
        - oauth_auth:
            - write:users
            - read:users

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>In <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> on line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/>, the OpenAPI specification does not enforce encrypted communication.<AltParagraph>The OpenAPI specification does not enforce encrypted communication.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Unencrypted communication channels are prone to eavesdropping and tampering. Servicing client requests over an insecure communication channel allows attackers to perform man-in-the-middle attacks, and gives them access to read or modify the data in transit.
Description.Recommendations: Consider enabling transport encryption to ensure that all data exchange is performed over encrypted channels and inhibit man-in-the-middle attacks.

Description.Explanation: An API operation has been detected that allows credentials to travel over an unencrypted channel. OpenAPI security requirements and target servers definitions for an API operation will always override the respective global settings. However, when these settings are not defined for an operation, they default to the globally specified values.
Description.Recommendations: Always exchange sensitive information over a secure communication channel. Consider changing the communication scheme to HTTPS or protecting the data through an alternate approach that is appropriate to your system's requirements.

Description.Abstract: In on line , the OpenAPI specification is missing the securitySchemes definition.The OpenAPI specification is missing the securitySchemes definition.
Description.Explanation:
The securitySchemes definition specifies the security mechanisms that may be used globally or by specific API operations. The securitySchemes definition is typically specified under the reusable components object and is referenced globally or by specific operations to dictate security requirements for interaction. Example 1: The following OpenAPI specification fails to define the securitySchemes definition. 
    openapi: 3.0.3
    info:
      title: My API
      version: 1.0.0
    components:
     schemas:
        GeneralError:
          type: object
            properties:
             ...
Description.Recommendations:
The securitySchemes definition provides the required information for securely interacting with API endpoints. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It includes the securitySchemes definition. 
    openapi: 3.0.3
    info:
      title: My API
      version: 1.0.0
    components:
     schemas:
        GeneralError:
          type: object
          properties:
           ...     
     securitySchemes:
        api_key:
            type: apiKey
            name: api_key
            in: header
        petstore_auth:
            type: oauth2
            flows: 
        ...

Description.Abstract: In on line , the OpenAPI specification does not include a security definition for an API operation.The OpenAPI specification does not include a security definition for an API operation.
Description.Explanation:
API operations define security requirements to inform API consumers of the authentication and authorization parameters required to successfully invoke them. Operations that do not include a security definition might enable attackers to interact with sensitive API endpoints and allow them to perform actions that should be restricted to specific user accounts with explicit privileges. Example 1: The following OpenAPI specification fails to set a security definition for a sensitive operation. Additionally, without a global security definition, the createUsers operation is vulnerable to unauthorized and unauthenticated access. 
openapi: 3.0.0
info:
...
paths:
  /users:
    post:
      operationId: createUsers
      responses:
        '201':
        ...
Description.Recommendations:
security definitions provide the default authentication and authorization requirements for API operations. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It specifies a security definition for the createUsers operation. 
openapi: 3.0.0
info:
...
paths:
  /users:    
    post:
      operationId: createUsers
      security:
      - oauth_auth:
        - write:users
      responses:
        '201':
          ...

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>In <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> on line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/>, the OpenAPI specification makes security optional for an API operation.<AltParagraph>The OpenAPI specification makes security optional for an API operation.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
API operations define security requirements to inform API consumers of the authentication and authorization parameters required to successfully invoke them. Operations that make security optional might enable attackers to interact with sensitive API endpoints and allow them to perform actions that should be restricted to specific user accounts with explicit privileges. Example 1: The following OpenAPI specification makes security optional by including an empty object {} in the security definition for a sensitive operation. This overrides globally defined security requirements and renders the createUsers operation vulnerable to unauthorized and unauthenticated access. 
openapi: 3.0.0
info:
...
paths:
  /users:
    post:
      operationId: createUsers
      security: 
      - {}
      - oauth_auth:
          - write:users
          - read:users
      responses:
        '201':
          ...
Description.Recommendations:
security definitions provide the default authentication and authorization requirements for API operations. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It specifies a security definition that has no optional entries on the createUsers operation. 
    openapi: 3.0.3
    info:
      title: My API
      version: 1.0.0
    security:
        - oauth_auth:
          - write:users
          - read:users

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>In <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> on line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/>, the OpenAPI specification does not define responses for security-relevant status codes for an operation that uses an authentication scheme.<AltParagraph>The OpenAPI specification does not define responses for security-relevant status codes for an operation that uses an authentication scheme.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Always configure APIs to use custom error responses instead of relying on the underlying framework's default responses. Default responses might give detailed information about the error that occurred, and inadvertently leak sensitive information.
Attackers may leverage the additional information provided by a default error response to mount attacks targeting the framework, database, or other resources used by the API.
Description.Recommendations: Make sure the specification provides 401 and 403 status code response definitions for security-sensitive operations. RFC 2616 for the HTTP protocol requires a 401 response when client authentication is missing or cannot be performed using the provided credentials. The specification also requires a 403 response if the client is not authorized to access the requested resource.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a configuration does not specify a customer-managed encryption key for data at rest.<AltParagraph>A configuration does not specify a customer-managed encryption key for data at rest.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Customer-managed keys are not used to encrypt data at rest.
By default, AWS uses AWS-managed keys to encrypt data at rest if encryption is enabled. Customer-managed keys enable organizations to use cryptographic keys of their choice to encrypt data. This gives organizations better control over and logging of encryption processes.
As such, customer-managed keys are often part of the solution to address requirements that include but are not limited to: - Audit logs for sensitive data access - Data residency - Replacing, disabling, or destroying keys
Note that keys with the format aws/service-name are reserved for AWS-managed keys.
Description.Recommendations:
For more control over the encryption process of sensitive data, configure customer-managed keys to encrypt data at rest.
Using customer-managed keys requires organizations to fully manage key lifecycle activities including issuance, storage, revocation, and rotation.
Organizations should review their compliance requirements and determine whether to use customer-managed keys.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, a configuration defines a network rule with overly broad access permissions.<AltParagraph>A configuration defines a network rule with overly broad access permissions.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Loose access configurations can expose systems and broaden an organization's attack surface. Services open to interaction with the public are typically subjected to near-continuous scanning and probing by malicious entities.
This is especially problematic when a zero-day exploit for an exposed service is discovered and published, such as Heartbleed. Attackers can actively pursue and search for unpatched and exposed systems to exploit.
Description.Recommendations:
Define network rules that restrict access to services and ensure the services are available to as limited an audience as possible.
For example, do not make ports for service management activities publicly accessible. Ensure these ports are only available to a restricted pool of systems that require authorized access.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>On line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/>, an Azure service does not use customer-managed keys.<AltParagraph>An Azure service does not use customer-managed keys.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation: Mismanaged encryption keys are the cause of various security breaches. Organizations should not rely on platform-managed keys for critical data resources.
Description.Recommendations:
By default, Azure leverages platform-managed keys (PMKs) to protect data.
Organizations can instead configure Azure services to use customer-managed keys (CMKs) to protect their data.
Specifically using CMKs enables organizations to:
- import HSM-generated keys - audit usage of keys - control access to keys - cancel, revoke, or rotate keys
Using CMKs requires organizations to fully manage key lifecycle activities including issuance, storage, revocation, and rotation.
Organizations should review their compliance requirements and determine whether to use customer-managed keys.

Description.Explanation:

Configuration settings that undermine logging capabilities include but are not limited to: - deliberately disabling audit logging - exempting actions of specific users, groups, or processes from being logged - inadequately protecting log integrity - not enabling optional audit logging - reducing the log sampling rate

Descriptions.Explanation:
By default, Azure Storage Accounts allow cross-tenant replication. This provides a data-exfiltration means for attackers that have access to create an Azure Storage Account Object Replication Policy. Example 1: The following example template defines an Azure Storage Account that allows cross-tenant replication. 
{
    "type": "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts",
    "apiVersion": "2021-06-01",
    "name": "[parameters('storageAccountName')]",
    ...
    "properties": {
        "allowCrossTenantReplication": true,
        ..
}

By default, Azure Cosmos DB data is encrypted using Microsoft service-managed keys. However, organizations can also apply a second layer of encryption by providing a Customer-Managed Key (CMK). Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines a Cosmos DB Account with no customer-managed key to further protect the data at rest. 
resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "test" {
  name                = "example-cosmosdb-account"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.test.name
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.test.location
  offer_type          = "Standard"
...
}

By default, Azure Storage Account data is encrypted using an account encryption key. However, organizations can also specify a customer-managed key that is used to encrypt and control access to the key that is used to encrypt storage data. Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an Azure Storage Account without a customer-managed key to encrypt the data encryption key. 
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "test" {
  name                     = "storageaccountname"
  resource_group_name      = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  location                 = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "GRS"    
}
Example 2: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an Azure Storage Account Encryption Scope that uses a Microsoft service-managed key to encrypt the data encryption key. 
resource "azurerm_storage_encryption_scope" "aztf003-tp-02" {
  name               = "microsoftmanaged"
  storage_account_id = azurerm_storage_account.aztf003-tp-02.id
  source             = "Microsoft.Storage"
}

Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines a container registry without a customer-managed key. 
resource "azurerm_container_registry" "test" {
  name                = "containerRegistryTest"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
}

Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an AKS cluster without a customer-managed key to encrypt the OS and data disks. 
resource "azurerm_kubernetes_cluster" "example-aks-aztp01" {
  name                = "example-aks-aztn01"
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  dns_prefix          = "exampleaks1"
  default_node_pool {
    name       = "default"
    node_count = 1
    vm_size    = "Standard_D2_v2"
  }
}

Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an Azure VM without a disk encryption set to encrypt the OS and data disks. 
resource "azurerm_linux_virtual_machine" "aztf006tp001" {
  name                            = "aztf006tp001-vm"
  resource_group_name             = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  ...
  os_disk {
    storage_account_type = "Standard_LRS"
    caching              = "ReadWrite"
  }
  ...
}

Example 1: The following example shows a Terraform configuration that defines an Azure managed disk that does not use customer-managed keys for encryption. 
resource "azurerm_managed_disk" "aztf007-tp-001" {
  name                 = "aztf007-tp-001"
  location             = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  resource_group_name  = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  storage_account_type = "Standard_LRS"
  create_option        = "Empty"
  disk_size_gb         = "1"
  encryption_settings {}
}

In this case, a CloudTrail log is not integrated with CloudWatch Logs, which results in less visibility and reduced ability to respond to security-related incidents. CloudWatch Logs provide a way to monitor CloudTrail logs for security-relevant events and raise alerts to concerned parties so they can take appropriate action. Example 1: The following template defines an AWS trail without defining an appropriate CloudWatchLogsLogGroupArn. 
myTrail:
DependsOn:
    - BucketPolicy
Type: AWS::CloudTrail::Trail
Properties:
    S3BucketName:
        Ref: S3Bucket
        IsLogging: true

Example 1: The following template defines a trail that is not enabled for all regions. You can either configure this explicitly as shown or by omission of the IsMultiRegionTrail property. 
"myTrail": {
    "DependsOn": [
        "BucketPolicy"
    ],
    "Type": "AWS::CloudTrail::Trail",
    "Properties": {
        "S3BucketName": {
            "Ref": "S3Bucket"
        },
        "IsLogging": true,
        "IsMultiRegionTrail": false
    }
}

Example 1: The following template defines a trail that is not enabled for all regions. You can either configure this explicitly as shown or by omission of the IsMultiRegionTrail property. 
myTrail:
  DependsOn:
    - BucketPolicy
  Type: AWS::CloudTrail::Trail
  Properties:
    S3BucketName:
      Ref: S3Bucket
      IsLogging: true
      IsMultiRegionTrail: false

By default, CloudFront does not require that viewers use HTTPS so connections are not encrypted when CloudFront communicates with viewers. An attacker residing on a shared network might be able to snoop and tamper with unencrypted traffic. Example 1: The following example shows an Ansible task that fails to enforce secure end-to-end connections between a CloudFront distribution and viewers because viewer_protocol_policy is set to allow-all. 
- name: Create a basic distribution with an origin
  community.aws.cloudfront_distribution:
    state: present
    ...
    default_cache_behavior:
      viewer_protocol_policy: allow-all

The Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocols provide a protection mechanism to ensure the authenticity, confidentiality, and integrity of data transmitted between a client and web server. Both TLS and SSL have undergone revisions that result in periodic version updates. Each new revision addresses security weaknesses discovered in the previous version. Use of an insecure version of TLS/SSL weakens the strength of the data protection and might allow an attacker to compromise, steal, or modify sensitive information. Insecure versions of TLS/SSL might exhibit one or more of the following properties: - No protection against man-in-the-middle attacks - Same key used for authentication and encryption - Weak message authentication control - No protection against TCP connection closing The presence of these properties might enable an attacker to intercept, modify, or tamper with sensitive data. Example 1: The following Ansible task sets the minimum SSL/TLS protocol that CloudFront uses to communicate with viewers to SSLv3. As a result, viewers can use one of the outdated SSL/TLS protocols, which includes SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1, to connect to a CloudFront distribution. 
- name: Create a basic distribution with an origin
  community.aws.cloudfront_distribution:
    state: present
    default_origin_domain_name: www.cloudfront.example.com
    viewer_certificate:
      minimum_protocol_version: SSLv3

Descriptions.Recommendations:
Disable cross-tenant replication for Azure Storage Accounts that do not need this capability. This can be configured with apiVersions 2021-04-01 and later using the allowCrossTenantReplication property. Example 2: The following example fixes the problem in Example 1. It defines an Azure Storage Account that prevents cross-tenant replication. 
{
    "type": "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts",
    "apiVersion": "2021-06-01",
    "name": "[parameters('storageAccountName')]",
    ...
    "properties": {
        "allowCrossTenantReplication": false,
        ..
}

Customer-managed keys provide an added layer of protection to the data stored by Azure Cosmos DB. Example 2: The following example improves the configuration in Example 1. It specifies a customer-managed key for Cosmos DB to perform double encryption of data at rest. 
resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "test" {
  name                = "example-cosmosdb-account"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.test.name
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.test.location
  offer_type          = "Standard"
  key_vault_key_id    = azurerm_key_vault_key.generated.id
  ...
}

Consider adding a customer-managed key to provide an added layer of protection to the data stored by the Azure Storage Account. Example 3: The following example improves the configuration in Example 1. It specifies a customer-managed key to encrypt the data encryption key. 
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "test" {
  name                     = "storageaccountname"
  resource_group_name      = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  location                 = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "GRS"
  customer_managed_key {
     key_vault_key_id          = azurerm_key_vault.example.id
     user_assigned_identity_id = data.azurerm_client_config.current.object_id
  }
}
Example 4: The following example improves the configuration in Example 2. It specifies a customer-managed key to encrypt the data encryption key of the Azure Storage Account Encryption Scope. 
resource "azurerm_storage_encryption_scope" "aztf003-tn-02" {
  name               = "customermanaged"
  storage_account_id = azurerm_storage_account.aztf003-tn-02.id
  source             = "Microsoft.KeyVault"
  key_vault_key_id          = azurerm_key_vault.example.id
}

By default, Azure Container Registry content is encrypted using Microsoft service-managed keys. Consider using customer-managed keys to protect container registry contents. Example 2: The following improves the configuration in Example 1. It specifies a customer-managed key for the container registry. 
resource "azurerm_container_registry" "test" {

To block public access of S3 data and to forbid anyone from adding policies or ACLs that grant public access, set both block_public_policy and block_public_acls to yes in the public_access parameter of Ansible amazon.aws.s3_bucket plugin. To also guard against any pre-existing overly-permissive bucket policies and ACLs, set both restrict_public_buckets and ignore_public_acls to yes. Example 2: The following Ansible task creates an AWS S3 bucket and enables all S3 Block Public Access settings. 
- name: setup an s3bucket
  amazon.aws.s3_bucket:
    name: demos3bucket
    state: present
    public_access:
    block_public_policy: yes
    restrict_public_buckets: yes
    block_public_acls: yes
    ignore_public_acls: yes

To block public access of S3 data and to forbid anyone from adding policies or ACLs that grant public access, set the property PublicAccessBlockConfiguration, under the AWS S3 Bucket, and assign true to all of the following settings: BlockPublicAcls IgnorePublicAcls BlockPublicPolicy RestrictPublicBuckets Example 1:An S3 bucket with all S3 Block Public Access settings. 
...
Resources:
  AWSS3Bucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
...

Ensure that every CloudFront distribution is configured to enforce secure end-to-end connections to viewers by including a viewer_protocol_policy parameter under default_cache_behavior. Also set all instances of the viewer_protocol_policy parameter to either https-only or redirect-to-https. Example 2: The following Ansible task configures a CloudFront distribution to deliver contents via HTTPS by default. All connections for the contents in the specific path named /foo/bar are redirected from HTTP to HTTPS. 
- name: Create a basic distribution with an origin
  community.aws.cloudfront_distribution:
    state: present
    ...
    default_cache_behavior:
      viewer_protocol_policy: https-only
    ...
    cache_behaviors:
      - target_origin_id: 'test origin-123456'
        path_pattern: /foo/bar
        viewer_protocol_policy: redirect-to-https
    ...
